blocks.text: From Condition Assessment to State-Evolution Control: A Critical Review and Dual-Loop Framework for Intelligent Railway Infrastructure O&M
Abstract:

The global expansion of high-speed and heavy-haul railway networks has shifted the industry focus from large-scale construction to long-term sustainable operation and maintenance (O&M). However, traditional O&M models face critical bottlenecks, including the "spatial-temporal blind spots" in macroscopic inspections, the "surface-only" limitation of sensing technologies, and the reactive nature of maintenance decision-making. This paper provides a systematic review of the transition from traditional maintenance to an AI-empowered "State Evolution" philosophy. First, we analyze the inherent constraints of existing systems in perception, assessment, and execution. Second, an engineering-oriented dual-loop top-level architecture is proposed: the first loop constitutes an AI-driven full-process intelligent O&M closed loop, ensuring comprehensive perception and holistic health characterization; while the second loop serves as a precision intervention loop, leveraging AI agents and automated robotics for targeted execution. The feasibility of this framework is demonstrated through practical engineering case studies, including the Dazhun Heavy-Haul Railway and the development of multi-sensor integrated inspection robots. These cases illustrate a paradigm shift from "evaluating current states" to "predicting future deterioration". Finally, this study outlines future trajectories for AI integration, providing a theoretical and practical roadmap for the next generation of intelligent railway O&M systems.
Keywords: Railway Infrastructure; Intelligent Operation and Maintenance; State Evolution; Artificial Intelligence; Predictive Maintenance.

To characterize the research landscape at the intersection of railway infrastructure O&M and artificial intelligence, this review combines bibliometric mapping with critical synthesis. A bibliometric search was conducted in the Scopus database, targeting publications that jointly addressed railway infrastructure, operation and maintenance, and intelligent technologies. The search terms combined four groups of keywords: railway systems (“railway”, “railroad”, “high-speed railway”, “heavy-haul railway”), infrastructure assets (“track”, “bridge”, “tunnel”, “subgrade”, “ballast”, “slab track”, “fastening”), O&M activities (“inspection”, “condition monitoring”, “maintenance”, “predictive maintenance”, “asset management”), and intelligent technologies (“artificial intelligence”, “machine learning”, “deep learning”, “digital twin”, “robot”, “large language model”, “agent”). The search was last updated in June 2026 and was used to identify publication trends, citation growth, and major research concentrations in this field.

As shown in Figure 3, the application of AI technology in railway O&M has experienced rapid growth over the past decade. The annual number of publications follows an exponential growth trajectory, with a fitted curve equation of and a coefficient of determination of . Prior to 2013, research in this interdisciplinary field progressed at a relatively steady pace; however, with the rapid development of deep learning, big data analytics, and intelligent sensing technologies, the number of related publications began to increase sharply after 2015. Cumulative citations have also grown substantially, indicating the increasing influence of this topic in both academic research and engineering practice.

For the qualitative synthesis, the bibliometric corpus was further screened and supplemented by backward and forward citation tracing. Studies were retained if they addressed railway infrastructure sensing and inspection, condition assessment, track geometry degradation, rail and ballast defects, predictive maintenance, maintenance planning and scheduling, data-driven or physics-informed modelling, digital twins, AI-enabled decision support, robotic inspection or maintenance, or post-maintenance verification. Studies focusing mainly on rolling stock, signalling, train control, passenger service, or generic algorithm development without a clear railway infrastructure O&M application were excluded from the main synthesis. In addition, highly relevant standards, books, technical reports, and foundational AI studies were included where they supported the conceptual framework or methodological discussion.

Railway Lines and Their Unique Features
The Unique Characteristics of Railway Lines
As a critical component of the nation’s transportation infrastructure, railway lines possess an irreplaceable uniqueness due to their operating environment and load characteristics:

Long-distance, large-scale linear projects that traverse complex geological and climatic zones. The modern high-speed rail network spans a vast area, and individual train trips are lengthy. For example, the Lanzhou-Xinjiang Railway in China spans a total length of 2,423 kilometers, traversing extremely complex and diverse terrain—including the Gobi Desert and mountain gorges—and is constantly exposed to harsh weather conditions such as extreme temperature fluctuations and frequent sandstorms (Luan and Liu, 2025). This vast geographical and climatic diversity poses severe environmental challenges for the railway infrastructure.

The direct medium for wheel-rail interaction, with extremely high safety sensitivity. Railway tracks are directly subjected to the immense dynamic forces generated by high-speed trains. Even the slightest defect in the track geometry or physical properties can be significantly amplified by the high-speed interaction between the wheels and the rails, which not only causes severe system vibrations but also poses a direct threat to train safety and passenger comfort. In the past few years, train derailments caused by severe track defects have occurred in many parts of the world (Ouyang et al., 2010; Kim and Yoon, 2013) , clearly demonstrating the critical safety implications of track defects.

The distribution of diseases exhibits significant spatial randomness and discontinuity. The occurrence of railway track defects does not follow a uniform distribution pattern. It is influenced by local factors such as variations in subgrade settlement, structural discontinuities at switches and transition sections, and specific maintenance histories (Nabochenko et al., 2019; Wang, Liu and Euston, 2023a). Track geometric irregularities typically exhibit a high degree of spatial randomness and diverse short-wavelength discrete characteristics (Jin et al., 2025).

The disease spreads rapidly, and current detection methods have “blind spots”. Under the combined effects of high speeds and heavy loads, the track substructure—such as the ballast—deteriorates at an extremely rapid rate. At the same time, extreme weather conditions can easily trigger sudden structural failures, such as thermal separation at the track slab interfaces caused by high summer temperatures (Davies and Andrews, 2021), or frost heave in the subgrade caused by low winter temperatures. However, existing comprehensive inspection trains or manual inspections are conducted at limited intervals (such as every two weeks or once a month), making it highly likely that monitoring blind spots will arise during the intervals between inspections. In addition, the growing number of overnight trains that depart in the evening and arrive in the morning creates a serious conflict with the traditional nighttime maintenance window (12:00 a.m.–6:00 a.m.), further limiting the time and space available for track inspection and maintenance (T. Zhang et al., 2025).
Railway Lines

Railway tracks are highly complex linear structures primarily composed of the track superstructure and substructure. Depending on the type of track structure, there are significant differences in their components and mechanisms of condition evolution. They are mainly classified into ballasted and ballastless tracks.

Ballasted Track: the superstructure of a ballasted track primarily consists of rails (which provide guidance and bear the load), the fastening system (which connects the rails to the sleepers), and sleepers (which anchor the rails to the subgrade). The substructure, meanwhile, comprises granular layers such as ballast, sub-ballast, subgrade, and embankment. (Sun et al., 2023a; Koohmishi et al., 2024a). It should be noted that, depending on the perspective, the ballast layer can be classified as part of either the superstructure (Indraratna et al., 2016; Christos N. Pygidis, 2022) or the substructure (Selig and Waters, 1994; Christos N. Pygidis, 2022). Within railway granular ballast, ballast is the most vulnerable component and also plays a key role in adjusting track geometry (Koohmishi et al., 2024a). Under the high-frequency cyclic loads of trains, ballast is highly susceptible to initial compaction, aggregate fragmentation, and deformation-induced degradation. Combined with the intrusion of contaminants such as coal dust, this further exacerbates permanent deformation, directly leading to track geometric irregularities and subsequently accelerating the deterioration of other components (Liu and Xiao, 2010; Huang and Tutumluer, 2011; Lee et al., 2018; Meng et al., 2020).

Ballastless Track: Ballastless tracks offer good overall structural stability; the ballast layer has been eliminated and replaced with a solid foundation consisting of concrete track slabs, a cement-asphalt mortar layer, and a concrete base (Gautier, 2015; Grützmacher, Kang and Marx, 2025). However, the ride quality of ballastless tracks depends heavily on the precise condition of the fastening system (including fasteners and elastic pads). Due to the lack of elastic adjustment provided by ballast, maintenance can only be performed through millimeter-level track adjustments by modifying the thickness of the pads and the position of the fasteners at each sleeper; moreover, because of the strong physical coupling constraints between adjacent fasteners, the scope for adjustment is extremely limited (Sun et al., 2023a).
Research Contribution

Currently, there is a wealth of literature reviewing the application of AI technology in the railway field. We have reviewed comprehensive articles discussing the application of AI technology in the railway sector over the past four years. As shown in Table 1, these articles cover a wide range of topics, including both specialized studies focused on track defect detection and maintenance, as well as comprehensive reviews that provide an overview of the entire field. However, unlike previous reviews that focused on summarizing AI algorithms and technological applications, the objective of this paper is not merely to list the current state of AI applications in the railway sector, but rather to conduct an in-depth analysis of the underlying limitations of existing O&M systems and to explore practical engineering scenarios for the effective implementation of AI technology.

blocks.text: Research Objectives

This paper pursues four objectives: (1) To systematically review and analyze the inherent limitations of traditional railway operation and maintenance systems in areas such as perception, assessment, and execution. (2) To propose and justify a dual-loop intelligent O&M architecture that integrates an AI-driven decision loop — spanning the full infrastructure lifecycle — with a highly automated physical execution loop. (3) To evaluate the feasibility and performance of the proposed architecture through engineering case studies drawn from operational long-distance railway lines. (4) To identify open research challenges and outline a development roadmap for AI-driven intelligent O&M in large-scale railway networks.
Section Description

The subsequent sections of this paper are organized as follows: Section 2 analyzes the inherent limitations of existing railway operation and maintenance systems, discussing bottlenecks in current sensing, precise measurement, condition assessment, and traditional maintenance methods. Section 3 elaborates on the design logic and key technologies of the “dual-loop” intelligent operation and maintenance system, including the artificial intelligence decision-making loop covering the entire lifecycle and the highly automated precise execution loop. Section 4 evaluates the deployment and performance of the AI methods reviewed in Section 3 through engineering case studies drawn from operational railway lines. Finally, Section 5 summarizes the main research conclusions of this paper and outlines future development directions in the field of intelligent railway O&M.

blocks.text: Among them, surface defects such as rail surface damage, slab track cracks, and missing fastening systems can be explicitly detected via visual inspection or various types of sensing signals including images, giving rise to a series of non-contact, non-destructive precision detection technologies such as eddy current testing (Peng,Jianping, 2017), magnetic flux leakage testing (Wang et al., 2023), and visual inspection (Zhang,Xiangyang and Luo,Jiangping, 2021). The limitations of each single-source method are summarized in Table 2. In brief: eddy current testing is restricted to conductive surfaces and is sensitive to rail roughness; magnetic flux leakage is susceptible to rust and surface contamination; visual inspection cannot resolve subsurface damage or provide depth information. These individual limitations motivate multi-source fusion approaches.

Obviously, defect detection methods based on a single data source suffer from a high missed detection rate, which will inevitably cause continuous degradation of the dynamic performance of rails, worsen train running quality, and even induce potential safety hazards. With long-term service of line infrastructures, deep-seated defects such as rail fractures, ballast consolidation, and subgrade voids will occur in track structures. These hidden defects lack obvious external characteristics at the initial formation stage; if not identified in a timely manner, they will accumulate under long-term dynamic loads and trigger abrupt changes in structural stiffness or even local instability. Most precision measurement technologies for such conditions rely on non-destructive non-contact testing methods such as radar or electromagnetic waves to obtain "indirect signals" reflecting structural states. For example, in the detection of internal rail defects, ultrasonic testing (Han，Xue and Su，Huilong, 2021) is one of the most widely used non-destructive testing methods at present, with advantages including strong penetration capability, high sensitivity, low cost, rapid detection, and harmlessness to human bodies. Ultrasonic testing exploits differential sound-wave propagation to locate and size internal defects (Hu,Jinping and Ren,Jianping, 2006). Current limitations — low precision in vehicle-mounted systems, low speed in portable units, and incomplete cross-sectional coverage — are detailed in Table 2.

In ballast detection, ground penetrating radar (GPR) is one of the important means for detecting the internal conditions of slab tracks or ballast layers. It features rapid detection, non-destructiveness, and continuous data acquisition; vehicle-mounted GPR further offers the advantages of simple operation, high detection speed, and no interference with train operation, effectively solving the difficulty in rapidly and continuously acquiring ballast condition data for existing lines (Wang，Shilei et al., 2023). Its fundamental principle is that a transmitting antenna emits electromagnetic waves into the ballast; when the waves encounter regions with different dielectric properties, reflection and scattering occur, and a receiving antenna records the relevant signals to form A-scan and B-scan data. The basic condition of the ballast is then judged by analyzing differences in the data (Huang,Xing, 2022). Meanwhile, relevant explorations mainly focus on ballast cleanliness, interlayer structures, and local defect identification. Signal feature and data processing methods such as time-frequency analysis (Yu and Wang, 2016), machine learning(Hao, 2009), and deep learning (Xu, Zhang and Sun, 2021) have been successively introduced into the interactive process of "structural defect characteristics–radar signal processing", promoting the gradual extension of related technologies toward refined perception of multiple types of internal conditions of ballast layers.

GPR limitations include multi-path effects from ballast granular media, reliance on manual signal interpretation, and blurred defect boundaries in slab-track applications — see Table 2 for a structured comparison.

The interaction of the above two types of defects manifests as track alignment deviation and deterioration of track geometry on the line, causing irreversible damage to line infrastructure operations and potential operational risks. As the most intuitive indicators reflecting the overall condition of long-distance lines, the measurement of track geometry and irregularities is critical. At present, a relatively mature technical system for broadband track smoothness perception has been developed. For example, absolute measurement technology (Y. Wang et al., 2024) takes the operation and maintenance control network—one of the high-speed railway inspection and control networks—as a reference benchmark. Through the collaboration of "CPIII control points–total station–track inspection vehicle", it can accurately acquire multi-dimensional information such as spatial coordinates, track geometry deviation, and long-wave irregularities, but its measurement speed is generally 0.3~0.5 km/h. To further improve the efficiency of this technical approach, a series of new technologies have been derived, including self-levelling-free total stations, GNSS/InSAR integrated inertial navigation measurement (Parizzi, Gonzalez and Brcic, 2020), etc.

In addition, relative measurement technology based on the chord measurement method indirectly characterizes the actual track irregularity state through the relative positional relationship between different points on the measuring chord, enabling compatibility with shorter wavelength ranges. Since it does not require acquisition of absolute spatial coordinates, its maximum measurement speed can generally reach more than 3 km/h (YAZAWA and TAKESHITA, 2002). It is generally classified into three categories: mid-chord , eccentric chord , and multi-point chord , covering detection objects such as rail corrugation, joint irregularities, and medium-short wavelength irregularities.

In the context of modern railway infrastructure management, "census measurement" refers to the long-term, long-distance, and full-life-cycle inspection of the track network. This macroscopic evaluation is predominantly executed by dedicated Track Geometry Cars or Track Recording Vehicles, which provide continuous, high-speed, and non-destructive evaluations of the track's condition. While macroscopic census techniques provide essential network-level health screening, their architecture is not designed for localized, microscopic diagnostics. As networks evolve toward higher traffic densities and heavier axle loads, four systemic limitation categories have emerged — summarized in Table 2 and Figure 5. These vulnerabilities not only compromise the reliability of track assessments but also severely hinder the transition toward proactive maintenance. Through a comprehensive review of existing literature, the inadequacies of current macroscopic census technologies can be systematically deconstructed across four critical dimensions: spatiotemporal resolution constraints, physical sensing disconnects, data aggregation flaws, and the resultant reactive maintenance trap.

Spatiotemporal Resolution Constraints. Running dedicated TRVs is operationally expensive and disruptive, forcing a constant conflict between safety inspections and commercial train services. These specialized vehicles require exclusive "track possessions," forcing infrastructure managers into a constant conflict between conducting safety inspections and maintaining profitable, regular commercial train services (Paixão, Fortunato and Calçada, 2019; Malekjafarian et al., 2023). Consequently, the frequency of network-wide census inspections is severely compressed. In reality, large-scale networks—such as the Dutch railway system—often limit these inspections to merely twice a year (Wang, Chang and Markine, 2018).

This extremely low-frequency paradigm inherently restricts census data to isolated, short-term "static snapshots," creating massive temporal blind spots. Track degradation is rarely a perfectly slow, linear process; it frequently manifests as rapid track degradation or sudden damages induced by extreme dynamic loads, severe weather, or sudden material fatigue (Malekjafarian et al., 2023). Because census measurements leave months-long gaps between consecutive inspections, they are fundamentally incapable of continuously monitoring active dynamic damage or providing early warnings for these sudden, highly critical localized failures (Shi et al., 2018).

Spatially, the macroscopic approach completely fails to support accurate full-life-cycle tracking of localized defects due to inherent positioning errors. Long-distance inspections rely heavily on mileage encoders and GPS, both of which are highly susceptible to wheel slip, route variations (e.g., changing lanes), and signal losses in tunnels or urban canyons (Wang et al., 2018). This vulnerability inevitably introduces cumulative "mileage drift" and spatial desynchronization across different batches of census data (Guo et al., 2025). Without absolute spatial synchronization, it is impossible to accurately evaluate the localized degradation rate of a specific defect over its lifecycle. Consequently, a defect recorded in one census might be misidentified as entirely new defect in the next, rendering long-term historical census data virtually useless for precise micro-maintenance (Wang et al., 2018).

Physical Sensing Disconnect. A critical load discrepancy exists between inspection vehicles (typically ~5 t axle load) and in-service trains (12–16 t). Standard inspection vehicles typically apply axle loads (e.g., 5 tonnes) that are significantly lighter than those of in-service passenger or heavy-haul freight trains (e.g., 12–16 tonnes). This severe load deficit means that structural defects highly sensitive to extreme dynamic loading—such as localized track stiffness degradation and dynamic settlement—remain unexcited and uncompressed during the census, leading to massive underestimations of the actual danger (OBrien et al., 2018).

Furthermore, traditional census sensors primarily scan the surface geometry of the rail head. This "surface blindness" means the system only records the ultimate symptoms of degradation, remaining completely blind to the underlying structural root causes, such as localized subgrade settlement, poor drainage, or ballast fouling (Zarembski, Grissom and Euston, 2014; Wang, Liu and Euston, 2023b). This physical sensing blind spot becomes exceptionally catastrophic at critical structural nodes, such as bridge-to-subgrade transition zones and switches and crossings (S&C). In transition zones, abrupt variations in vertical stiffness generate extreme dynamic impacts that damage track components long before surface geometry thresholds are breached (Heydari, 2024). Similarly, at complex S&C nodes, the inherent geometric discontinuities (physical gaps in the rail) not only render conventional automated sensors (e.g., eddy current or image recognition) ineffective, but also completely confound dynamic sensors, which struggle to separate normal structural gap impacts from actual defect-induced vibrations (Wei et al., 2017). By ignoring the true operational conditions and actual wheel-rail dynamic interactions, static geometry census fails to accurately quantify the state of these high-degradation nodes, forcing a reliance on inefficient manual visual inspections (Milosevic et al., 2022a).

Data Aggregation Flaws. High data volume does not equate to diagnostic accuracy: true defects are extremely sparse within the data, and macroscopic aggregation into indices such as TQI introduces a smoothing effect that masks localized failures. As railway mileage expands, single-node computing architectures face severe processing bottlenecks, causing unacceptable delays in generating track quality reports for frontline maintenance (Guo et al., 2025). More critically, the data collected is overwhelmingly imbalanced; the vast majority of the track is healthy, meaning true localized defects are extremely "sparse" within the data ocean (Hou, Zhao and Yang, 2023; Kim, Fernández-Bobadilla and Chen, 2023). This extreme sparsity, coupled with the sensors' vulnerability to environmental noise (e.g., sunlight, rain, electromagnetic interference) and the lack of precise physical labels, heavily degrades the reliability of automated machine learning classifiers, often necessitating slow and highly subjective expert interpretation (Hou, Zhao and Yang, 2023; Guo et al., 2025).

To manage this data explosion, industry practices mathematically aggregate track measurements into macroscopic indicators, such as the Track Quality Index (TQI), over fixed spatial segments (e.g., 200 meters). However, this macroscopic aggregation creates a dangerous "smoothing effect" that forcibly dilutes continuous defect boundaries and masks severe localized spot failures (Fontul et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2018). Furthermore, census systems generally evaluate defects of different wavelengths (e.g., long-wave track settlement and short-wave dipped joints) in total isolation. This arbitrary mathematical separation completely ignores the catastrophic "dynamic coupling amplification effects" that occur when these multi-wavelength defects overlap spatially, leading to severe misjudgments in maintenance priorities (Kaewunruen and Chiengson, 2018). The widespread use of chord measurement methods further exacerbates this by introducing Track Irregularity Conversion Errors (TICE), where the same physical defect yields entirely different severity scores depending on the chord's starting position (OBrien et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2023b). Ultimately, as El-khateeb et al dramatically highlight, a "normal" overall macroscopic condition index can be highly misleading—it often projects a false sense of security while successfully burying the imminent failure of a localized critical component, such as a severely deteriorated sleeper(2021).

Reactive Maintenance Trap. The cumulative effect of the three limitations above traps census-based systems in a threshold-exceedance model: interventions are triggered only after safety limits are breached. Because census data lacks the capability to continuously capture subsurface causal parameters (like ballast fouling and thickness), it is fundamentally devoid of true "forecasting power" (Yurlov et al., 2019). Consequently, interventions are almost exclusively triggered after safety limits have been breached, forcing infrastructure managers into a reactive ("wait until it degrades and then fix it") rather than proactive maintenance paradigm(Zarembski, Grissom and Euston, 2014).

Even when maintenance is initiated based on census alarms, the macroscopic nature of the data causes severe discrepancies during physical execution. Macroscopic maintenance planning often treats the track as a series of isolated points, completely ignoring the microscopic physical coupling constraints of adjacent track components, such as the stress linkage between adjacent fasteners (Sun et al., 2023b). Furthermore, blindly conducting localized interventions based purely on surface geometry alarms without addressing the underlying structural cause—such as aggressively tamping a section of track suffering from severe subgrade settlement—not only wastes immense resources but can mechanically accelerate track deterioration and ballast wear (Fontul et al., 2016).

blocks.text: Assessment and Decision-making
Track Status Assessment

Railways are the backbone of modern transportation systems, and the integrity of their infrastructure directly affects operational safety and transportation efficiency. According to statistics, infrastructure failures—including broken rails, ballast settlement, and bridge damage—are among the leading causes of railway accidents(Bianchi et al., 2025a). Traditional periodic manual inspections are no longer sufficient to meet the inspection needs of modern high-density, high-speed rail networks; as a result, automated, continuous, and intelligent condition assessment technologies have become a hot topic of research. The scope of railway condition assessment encompasses track structures (rails, fasteners, sleepers, ballast, and subgrade), bridge and tunnel structures, as well as functional equipment such as overhead contact systems and turnouts. The objectives of such assessments can be categorized into three areas: defect detection, condition grading, and degradation trend prediction, which correspond to the three maintenance strategies of reactive repair, condition-based maintenance, and predictive maintenance, respectively(Bris-Peñalver, Verdecia-Peña and Alonso, 2026a).
Track Geometry Condition Assessment

The core task of evaluating track geometry inspection data is to convert multidimensional measurements into quantifiable condition ratings to support maintenance decisions. Among the most widely used metrics are the Track Quality Index (TQI) and the Track Geometry Index (TGI), both of which are quantitative indicators that assess the condition of railway tracks by evaluating multiple geometric parameters (Safari Tarbozagh et al., 2026). The core significance of these two types of metrics lies in condensing the geometric dispersion of spatial distribution into a single management metric, thereby enabling the prioritized allocation of maintenance resources.

However, the degradation of the geometric condition is also related to changes in the support conditions of the ballast and subgrade; relying solely on the TQI or TGI makes it difficult to distinguish between different degradation mechanisms. Morais et al. (2023) proposed a method for assessing the condition of railway track supports based on modal analysis of the natural frequencies of multi-unit systems. This approach utilizes tools for monitoring and analyzing the natural frequencies of specific sections of the railway track to obtain information regarding the condition of the track support system—particularly the subgrade. By incorporating tensor decomposition analysis, Woldemariam and Attoh-Okine (2025) developed a joint model of multi-cycle geometric data and subgrade performance indicators, identifying spatial correlation degradation patterns that cannot be captured by the scalar TQI statistic—such as cyclic exceedances in specific mileage sections—and revealing the physical mechanism of localized support instability rather than global uniform degradation.
Internal Rail Defect Assessment

The objective of analyzing ultrasonic testing signals is to extract information regarding the location, size, and type of defects from the echo sequence, thereby establishing a quantitative mapping from “signal anomalies” to “defect grades.” Phased Array Ultrasonic Testing (PAUT) uses electronic scanning to cover multiple incidence angles in a single excitation; its S/B/C scan images directly display the distribution of reflection amplitudes within the cross-section, providing a richer information source for defect geometric reconstruction than single-probe A-scan testing (Garcia and Zhang, 2006; Phrommahakul et al., 2025).

Deep learning methods have significantly improved the efficiency of automated ultrasound image assessment(Islam and Olm, 2024; Lu et al., 2024). Related studies have demonstrated that the adoption of deep learning models enables the efficient and accurate identification of defects in track components in real-world scenarios, thereby helping to enhance the level of automated monitoring and maintenance of railway infrastructure.
Wheel–Rail Dynamic Condition Assessment

Vehicle-track dynamic models are widely used to analyze the response of the wheel-rail interface, axle boxes, or the vehicle body in order to assess track conditions and detect surface defects in the rails, or to analyze vertical and lateral wheel-rail forces based on the vehicle’s response (Yang et al., 2026). Early rail dynamics models were largely based on the theory of continuous elastic beams, simplifying the rail to an Euler-Bernoulli beam or a Timoshenko beam. These models combined a discrete elastic support model to simulate the track-bed support system and used analytical methods to solve for the coupled vibration response of heavy-haul vehicles and the track. For example, Chen et al. (2022) developed a vehicle-track coupled dynamic model capable of detecting track irregularities, ballast settlement, and fastener damage, thereby assessing the extent of track deterioration.

In addition to developing dynamic models, data-driven methods are also frequently employed to evaluate track conditions. Perrin et al. (2015) constructed a four-dimensional random field model of track irregularities to extract the probability density characteristics of vehicle responses. Masoomi and Jalili (2017) further developed a vehicle dynamics model that accounts for nonlinear suspension, revealing the statistical effects of random road irregularities on the system’s dynamic response.

However, purely data-driven methods for condition assessment and service life prediction generally suffer from insurmountable “black box” limitations. On the one hand, data models rely heavily on massive amounts of comprehensive, high-quality historical labeled data. In the complex and ever-changing operational environment of heavy-haul railways, where models must contend with severe noise interference, rare failures with small sample sizes, and unknown operating conditions, their generalization capabilities and robustness often face severe challenges. On the other hand, when performing feature extraction and trend inference, simple machine learning, deep neural networks, or large language models are completely detached from the inherent mechanical evolution mechanisms of the track system. This results in models that not only lack clear physical interpretability, but whose assessment decisions may even violate basic laws of dynamics and energy conservation. In the latter part of this section, we will explore a method for assessing the service condition of railway tracks based on a physical-information neural network (PINN).

From the perspective of technological evolution, one of the most significant changes in railway O&M lies in the transformation of data acquisition methods. Traditional maintenance mainly depends on manual patrols, periodic inspection vehicles, and field experience records, which often results in low-frequency, weakly structured, and fragmented data. These limitations make it difficult to support real-time diagnosis and long-term degradation prediction. In recent years, track inspection vehicles, onboard vibration sensors, wayside monitoring systems, machine vision, unmanned aerial vehicles, LiDAR, and Internet of Things devices have been increasingly applied to the monitoring of tracks, turnouts, bridges, tunnels, overhead contact systems, and rolling stock (Sedghi et al., 2021a). As a result, railway O&M data have become multi-source, heterogeneous, high-frequency, and strongly coupled in both space and time. More frequent, automated, and standardized inspection methods can improve the repeatability, consistency, and usability of maintenance data, thereby providing a foundation for machine learning and predictive maintenance (Bris-Peñalver, Verdecia-Peña and Alonso, 2026b).

In terms of condition diagnosis and health assessment, machine learning and deep learning methods have been widely used in railway track geometry degradation prediction, rail defect detection, turnout fault diagnosis, rolling stock anomaly detection, and overhead contact system condition assessment (Bai et al., 2015; Falamarzi, Moridpour and Nazem, 2019). Existing studies generally focus on data sources such as track geometry measurements, vibration responses, and image-based inspection data. Commonly used methods include support vector machines, random forests, artificial neural networks, deep learning models, and genetic algorithms(Mohammadi and He, 2022; Rodríguez-Hernández et al., 2025a). Compared with traditional statistical models, data-driven methods are capable of extracting complex degradation patterns from historical data. However, they still face several challenges, including unstable data quality, imbalanced samples, insufficient model interpretability, and limited generalization ability across different lines and operating conditions(Bris-Peñalver, Verdecia-Peña and Alonso, 2026b). For track geometry degradation prediction, machine learning has become an important research direction, but its engineering application still depends on high-quality historical inspection data, reasonable feature construction, and effective linkage between inspection records and maintenance records (Yingying Liao et al., 2022).

In the field of maintenance planning and scheduling, railway O&M needs to answer not only “where the fault is” and “when it may occur”, but also “when to maintain”, “how to maintain”, “which tasks should be prioritized”, and “which resources should be assigned”. Since railway maintenance is usually constrained by maintenance windows, line capacity, construction resources, equipment accessibility, and train operation plans, maintenance decision-making has typical characteristics of combinatorial optimization (Sedghi et al., 2021a). Existing studies have regarded railway track maintenance planning and scheduling as a multi-level decision-making problem, involving strategic asset renewal, tactical maintenance task arrangement, and operational scheduling of maintenance windows, personnel, and equipment. Although optimization models, heuristic algorithms, and decision support frameworks have been widely adopted, further improvements are still needed in terms of multi-component coupling, dynamic uncertainty, and practical engineering feasibility (Bressi, Santos and Losa, 2021).

With the development of digital technologies, railway O&M is evolving from single-equipment condition prediction toward system-level asset management. Digital O&M is not simply the electronic transformation of paper-based records. Instead, it integrates equipment condition, maintenance history, operation plans, risk levels, and resource allocation into a unified information framework through technologies such as big data, the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence, BIM/GIS, and digital twins (Rodríguez-Hernández et al., 2025b). Digital technologies can support the integration of condition monitoring, fault prediction, maintenance optimization, and strategic asset management. However, their effective implementation depends not only on algorithms, but also on railway organizational processes, technical standards, and asset management objectives. This indicates that the key to intelligent railway O&M is not merely improving model accuracy, but establishing a closed-loop management process involving condition perception, risk assessment, maintenance decision-making, and operational feedback .

In recent years, digital twin technology has been regarded as an important development direction for intelligent railway O&M. A digital twin can connect the physical railway system, real-time monitoring data, degradation models, and maintenance decision models, thereby providing a dynamic simulation environment for condition inference, fault warning, and maintenance scheme evaluation (Mutlu and Kaewunruen, 2026). Nevertheless, many current railway digital twin studies still remain at the level of digital representation or one-way monitoring platforms. A truly interactive, self-correcting, and closed-loop digital twin system has not yet been fully realized. In addition, although sustainability is frequently emphasized in railway maintenance studies, quantitative evaluation of green indicators such as carbon emissions, energy consumption, and environmental benefits remains insufficient.

Railway maintenance research has developed along two connected lines. The first line is a safety-governed engineering tradition: track condition is measured, compared with management or safety thresholds, and translated into inspection, repair, renewal or traffic-control actions. The second line is a model-supported decision tradition: degradation, recovery, risk and cost are estimated so that maintenance can be prioritized and scheduled more effectively. These traditions should not be treated as opposing paradigms. In railway infrastructure, a maintenance decision remains accountable only when it can be related to standards, asset condition, train-running safety, work possession, and post-work verification. Consequently, the literature is best read as a gradual movement from condition description to state evolution and from planning intent to executable intervention(Figure 1).

For long-distance railways, the key difficulty is that the asset is linear, geographically exposed, heterogeneous in track form and support condition, and strongly constrained by traffic windows. Network-level inspection can reveal where the state may be abnormal, but it often cannot determine the local physical cause, the exact repair boundary, or the expected repair effect. The present section therefore reviews existing research in four compact groups. Section 2.3.1 discusses safety governance and planning logic; Section 2.3.2 reviews predictive-maintenance pipelines; Section 2.3.3 summarizes deterioration and restoration mechanisms; and Section 2.3.4 examines component-specific and execution-oriented research. This arrangement separates what the literature has already established from the second-loop concept proposed later in Section 3.2.

Two remarks are necessary before the detailed review. First, existing maintenance research is highly mature in measurement, modelling and optimization, but the maturity is uneven across the maintenance chain. Inspection vehicles, geometry standards, degradation models and scheduling optimization have reached an advanced stage, while automated local repair and effect verification are still less developed. Second, the literature often uses the same term, predictive maintenance, for different decision levels. Some studies predict the next exceedance of a geometry threshold; others estimate component failure risk, remaining useful life, work cost or renewal timing. In this review, these outputs are interpreted according to their position in the O&M chain. A forecast that ranks sections belongs to network-level maintenance management; a forecast that chooses a local repair action and verifies its effect belongs to precision maintenance. This distinction is used consistently in the following subsections.
Safety governance, condition indices and maintenance planning

Railway maintenance is first a safety-governed activity. Geometry quality, rail integrity, support condition and component state are not simply descriptive variables; they are operational control variables linked to derailment risk, ride quality, traffic speed, comfort, availability and long-term asset cost. The traditional foundation of this governance is the use of track geometry parameters such as gauge, alignment, longitudinal level, cross-level and twist. These parameters are measurable at network scale and can be processed into isolated-defect indicators, standard deviations over fixed lengths, or composite quality indices. Early work on track-quality indices already showed that geometry statistics can summarize large sections, monitor degradation, and support maintenance-of-way planning (Hamid and Gross, 1981) Later studies developed statistical geometry indices based on field distributions and parameter weights, reinforcing the role of geometry as the most practical maintenance language(Sadeghi, 2010).

Modern standards keep this logic but make it more explicit. The EN 13848 series defines track geometry parameters, measurement characteristics and quality levels, including alert, intervention and immediate-action limits for geometric deviations (European Committee for Standardization, 2017). Chinese high-speed railway research similarly emphasizes the combined use of infrastructure-side management values and train-side safety limits. (Lu and Cai, 2020) argue that high-speed railway safety management should link the management value of track irregularity with train safety limits derived from dynamic criteria. This point matters because it prevents the maintenance system from becoming a purely statistical exercise: a small-looking irregularity may be relevant if it excites a vehicle-track dynamic response, whereas a larger deviation may be manageable when dynamic response and structural context are benign.

The same safety logic explains why railway decision-making remains hierarchical. Planning determines what work is required, where it is required, and how urgent it is. Scheduling converts that intent into feasible work packages under possession, resource, machine, crew and timetable constraints. (Sedghi et al., 2021b) show that the planning-scheduling distinction cannot be reduced only to time horizon; it also depends on the content of the decision, from maintenance interval selection and resource definition to possession allocation. For large-scale railway O&M, this distinction is crucial. A degraded section may be technically eligible for intervention long before the operator can obtain a possession window, assign a tamping or grinding machine, and coordinate adjacent tasks. Thus, maintenance intelligence is not only the ability to predict deterioration; it is also the ability to transform risk-ranked needs into auditable, deliverable work.

The limitation of this body of research is not that it is too conservative, but that it often stops at threshold crossing and work-list generation. Section-based indices are effective for governance, but they can hide short local defects, transition-zone deterioration, or component-specific mechanisms. Standards provide accountability, but they do not by themselves identify why a recurring geometry defect returns after repeated tamping. Planning and scheduling models improve cost and possession use, but many remain weakly coupled to field execution and post-work verification. These limitations motivate a two-layer view: existing research provides the first layer of safe and consistent maintenance governance, while future precision maintenance must add a second layer that closes the local intervention loop.

blocks.text: 2.3.2 Data-to-decision pipelines and predictive maintenance models

Predictive maintenance in railway infrastructure is not a single algorithmic task. It is a data-to-decision pipeline that converts heterogeneous observations into condition states, forecasts, work priorities and intervention rules. Reviews in the railway domain consistently distinguish between defect detection, diagnosis or classification, prognosis, and maintenance-decision coupling (Davari et al., 2021; Binder, Mezhuyev and Tschandl, 2023; Bianchi et al., 2025c). In track applications, the data sources include geometry measurements, ultrasonic testing, visual inspection, GPR, wayside monitoring, axle-load records, maintenance logs, traffic history, environmental exposure, and manually written inspection reports. This heterogeneity is useful, but it creates practical problems: the data are collected at different sampling rates, spatial resolutions and coordinate systems, and the labels used for model training are often indirect operational labels rather than true physical failure labels.

The first task is therefore alignment. Spatial alignment maps observations to a stable decision unit, such as a 200 m geometry unit, a rail segment, a switch, a level crossing or a transition-zone boundary. Temporal alignment links the current condition to deterioration history, cumulative tonnage, environmental events, previous repairs and post-maintenance recovery. Without these alignment steps, predictive models may appear accurate in statistical terms while remaining unusable for maintenance. For example, a model that forecasts deterioration over fixed equal-length sections may overlook a local transition-zone dip; a model that ignores previous tamping may overestimate the durability of restored geometry. Reviews of track geometry degradation and machine-learning prediction repeatedly emphasize that track quality is shaped by traffic, structure, maintenance history and local context (Higgins and Liu, 2018; Soleimanmeigouni, Ahmadi and Kumar, 2018; Y. Liao et al., 2022).

Methodologically, the literature can be grouped into four families. Statistical and stochastic models use regression, Markov chains, Weibull distributions, Wiener or Gamma processes, Bayesian methods and Monte Carlo simulation to represent deterioration and intervention timing. These models remain valuable because they are interpretable and can handle uncertainty. (Quiroga and Schnieder, 2012) and (Audley and Andrews, 2013) demonstrate how stochastic simulation and Petri-net formulations can represent track degradation, inspection, tamping and renewal as interacting processes. Machine-learning models, including random forests, support vector machines, neural networks and hybrid deep-learning architectures, have become more prominent as inspection datasets grow; (Y. Liao et al., 2022) review these models for track geometry degradation prediction. Physics-based and simulation-based models remain essential where labels are scarce but the vehicle-track mechanism is understood. Finally, hybrid models combine data-driven prediction with physical constraints or digital-twin simulation, a direction increasingly emphasized in recent railway infrastructure monitoring research (Bianchi et al., 2025c).

The most useful predictive outputs are not abstract accuracy scores. They are decision-ready quantities such as probability of threshold exceedance, time-to-limit, remaining useful life, defect recurrence risk, and prioritized work lists. (Caetano and Teixeira, 2016) show this principle in ballast tamping by linking degradation forecasting to a reliability-cost maintenance model. (Binder, Mezhuyev and Tschandl, 2023) similarly describes predictive maintenance as most deployable when it uses already available operational, inspection and maintenance data to support planning and scheduling rather than replace inspection. The implication is important for this review: predictive maintenance belongs primarily to the first closed loop when it screens and prioritizes the network; it enters the second loop only when the forecast is converted into a local repair target, an action, and a measurable acceptance criterion.

blocks.text: 2.3.3 Track deterioration, restoration and state evolution

The dominant state variable in track maintenance is geometry, but geometry is an effect rather than a complete cause. Geometry deterioration expresses how the rail-fastener-sleeper-support system evolves under repeated wheel loading, environmental exposure and previous interventions. In ballasted track, the central mechanism is the gradual loss of uniform support. Ballast settlement, particle breakage, abrasion, fouling, drainage degradation and subgrade weakening change the stiffness and damping of the track bed, leading to longitudinal-level and alignment irregularities. In this setting, tamping remains the main corrective operation because it directly restores sleeper support and rail position. Yet the recovery is imperfect and temporary. (Audley and Andrews, 2013) found that traffic speed and maintenance history affect subsequent deterioration and that tamping can damage ballast. This is why modern maintenance models treat tamping not as a reset to an as-new state, but as an intervention with limited and path-dependent recovery.

Slab and ballastless tracks follow a different maintenance logic. They are designed to avoid routine ballast rearrangement and to preserve high smoothness, but their defects are often related to structural interfaces, support conditions and environmental effects. (Ren et al., 2021) review Chinese high-speed slab-track research and highlight issues such as service performance evolution, damage maintenance standards, repair technologies and the need to evaluate maintenance effects. In slab systems, a geometry irregularity can correspond to concealed debonding, voiding, uneven settlement, frost heave, thermal deformation or interlayer degradation. Studies on CRTS III slab track under frost heave show that foundation deformation can lead to slab-track deformation and damage evolution (Cai et al., 2021). Hence the maintenance question is not simply whether a geometry threshold has been exceeded, but whether the observed geometry is a symptom of a deeper support or interface problem.

Rail and wheel-rail interface deterioration add another mechanism. Wear, corrugation, rolling contact fatigue, squats, head checks and profile evolution affect contact stress, dynamic loading, noise and vibration. Rail grinding and profile maintenance are therefore not only surface operations; they regulate the dynamic interaction that drives downstream track damage. Numerical wear-model reviews describe a standard chain in which multibody vehicle-track dynamics generates contact forces and creepages, contact mechanics resolves stresses, a wear law estimates material loss, and iterative profile updating predicts future profile evolution (Bosso, Magelli and Zampieri, 2022). Corrugation assessment based on wheel-rail forces and rail-grinding needs has also been studied as a way to connect measurement to grinding decisions (Niu et al., 2023).

Transition zones and discrete assets are another major source of state evolution. Bridges, culverts, tunnels, level crossings, turnouts and slab-ballast interfaces generate abrupt changes in stiffness, support condition or geometry. The resulting dynamic amplification produces differential settlement, local geometry loss and recurring maintenance demand. (Shang et al., 2021) argue that discrete rail assets require systems-thinking maintenance because they are short, numerous, heterogeneous and locally degraded, while (Shang et al., 2023) show how level crossings and associated transition zones can be optimized through surrogate-assisted dynamic design. The message for maintenance is clear: recurring defects should not be treated only by repeated geometry correction. Effective state-evolution management must identify whether the root cause lies in ballast fouling, sleeper support, rail profile, slab interface, drainage, stiffness transition or component failure.

2.3.4 Robotics and automated execution in railway maintenance

The fourth research direction concerns the physical execution of maintenance tasks. Compared with condition monitoring, deterioration modelling, and maintenance planning, automated execution remains the least mature part of railway infrastructure maintenance. Most existing systems can identify defects, rank risks, or support planning decisions, but the final intervention is still frequently performed by human crews or large maintenance machines under strict possession-window constraints. This creates a practical discontinuity in the data-to-maintenance chain: defects may be detected and prioritized digitally, while the repair action itself remains manual, weakly traceable, and difficult to verify in a closed-loop manner.

Recent autonomous railway platforms indicate a transition from inspection-centered automation toward execution-oriented maintenance. (J. Li et al., 2024) present a Railway Inspection and Maintenance Vehicle that integrates GPS, IMU, wheel encoders, LiDAR, depth camera, environmental camera, ROS2-based processing, remote monitoring, and emergency stop mechanisms. Although the reported validation mainly focuses on ultrasonic inspection, the system is important because it provides a modular mobile carrier for railway tasks. In other words, its value is not only defect sensing, but also the possibility of carrying different payloads, navigating along the rail corridor, and linking inspection data with field action. Such platforms provide the hardware basis for future automated intervention, particularly when local measurement, positioning, and task-specific tools can be integrated into the same vehicle.

Task-specific maintenance robots provide a more direct example of automated execution. (Guo, Zhang and Qi, 2019) develop a rail-fastener installation robot that combines visual recognition, sensor-based bolt localization, automatic feeding, manipulator control, and electric-wrench fastening under PLC control. This system is narrow in task scope, but it is highly relevant for precision maintenance because it demonstrates the full chain from perception to positioning and physical action. Fastener work is also a representative case of railway maintenance automation: the task is repetitive, spatially regular, safety-critical, and requires controlled torque or fastening quality. This makes it suitable for early robotic deployment before broader, less structured maintenance tasks can be automated.

Mobile manipulation is therefore a key bridge between inspection platforms and real repair robots. (Rahman et al., 2023) note that railway inspection technologies are more mature than robotic repair technologies, and that mobile manipulators are still rarely deployed in railway track maintenance. The difficulty lies not only in mechanical design but also in the railway working environment. Maintenance robots must operate under vibration, ballast unevenness, limited clearance, weather exposure, electromagnetic interference, strict safety requirements, and tight possession windows. They must also handle tools, materials, fasteners, or rail components with reliable localization and quality assurance. For this reason, future robotic maintenance is more likely to begin with constrained, task-specific operations rather than fully general autonomous repair.

Human-in-the-loop automation is another important path. Augmented reality and digital guidance technologies can support maintenance by providing visual instructions, spatial registration, and diagnostic guidance to operators. (Koh et al., 2020) show that AR-based maintenance for robots commonly relies on tracking, registration, and visual guidance, although many applications remain laboratory-based. In railway maintenance, such methods may be useful as transitional technologies. Before full robotic autonomy becomes reliable, AR-assisted execution can improve field consistency, reduce training demand, and connect human repair actions with digital work orders and inspection records. It also supports supervised automation, where a human operator monitors or confirms robotic action rather than performing the entire task manually.

Embodied AI provides the conceptual basis for more advanced robotic maintenance. (Sun et al., 2024) describe embodied intelligence as the integration of perception, cognition, and behavior through physical interaction with the environment. (Zheng et al., 2025) similarly organize embodied AI around perception, decision-making, and execution. These frameworks are relevant because railway maintenance robots cannot be treated as simple actuators. They must perceive the local track state, interpret the repair target, select an action strategy, execute it physically, and evaluate the resulting change. Object-centric robotic manipulation research further shows that reliable execution depends on pose estimation, affordance learning, policy learning, and task-oriented manipulation (Zheng et al., 2025). These capabilities are directly relevant to fine maintenance actions such as fastening, tool positioning, component replacement, surface treatment, and local adjustment.

Overall, the current literature suggests that railway maintenance automation is moving toward human-supervised, task-constrained, and verification-based robotics. The immediate goal is not unrestricted autonomy, but the formation of executable maintenance units: a robot or robotic platform should be able to reach the target site, localize the defect, perform a specific repair, measure the result, and report whether the intervention satisfies acceptance criteria. This execution logic is closely aligned with the second closed loop proposed in this review, where precision maintenance is realized through repeated measurement, decision, control, and re-measurement rather than through one-off repair.

blocks.text: Construction of the "Dual Closed-Loop" Intelligent O&M System

Confronting the core contradiction in railway infrastructure O&M — the inherent tension between full-network condition perception over large-scale line systems and the demands of precision, targeted maintenance execution — this paper proposes a "Dual Closed-Loop" architecture as the organizing framework for intelligent O&M.

The system comprises two functionally complementary and hierarchically progressive loops. The First Loop uses in-service commercial trains as sensing platforms; through continuous acquisition of on-board vibration and noise signals combined with AI-based inverse mapping models, it achieves low-cost, high-frequency dynamic condition census of the entire track network, with large model-assisted decision-making generating maintenance intervention commands — forming a full-process intelligent closed loop of "general sensing → condition assessment → decision output." The Second Loop takes precision inspection equipment as its data source; by fusing multi-source heterogeneous data from wideband geometric measurement, ground-penetrating radar, and distributed ground sensing networks, it achieves precise characterization of anomalous segments, and relies on unmanned precision maintenance technology to physically execute maintenance commands at high accuracy — forming an execution-layer closed loop of "precision sensing → precision maintenance → effect verification" .

The two loops operate in concert: the First Loop handles full-network screening and maintenance scheduling, while the Second Loop handles targeted diagnosis and precision execution, together achieving full-chain closure of intelligent railway O&M from sensing through decision-making to physical execution.
Figure Dual-loop architecture for intelligent railway infrastructure O&M: from census-level perception to precision maintenance
The First Loop: AI-Driven Full-Process Intelligent O&M Closed Loop

The core concept of the First Loop is to leverage the existing operational trajectories of in-service trains distributed across the railway network, transforming ordinary commercial vehicles into mobile sensing platforms with full-network coverage, achieving continuous and comprehensive track condition census at minimal marginal cost. This loop is supported by three progressively integrated technical modules: first, a multi-level vibration-noise sensing system combining IMUs and acoustic sensing establishes a high-quality onboard perception framework; second, deep generative learning methods address inevitable data gaps and noise through imputation and enhancement; and finally, AI-based inverse mapping models solve the core inverse problem of translating vehicle dynamic responses into track excitation states — converting vibration signals into track irregularity features that directly support O&M decision-making. Following condition assessment, the First Loop further incorporates a large language model-based intelligent decision-making module that transforms assessment outputs into structured maintenance scheduling commands, achieving full-chain closure across sensing, assessment, and decision-making.
Sensing Technology Enhancement

To address the inherent limitations of intermittent inspections by specialized Track Geometry Cars (TGCs), which often fail to capture the rapid deterioration of track quality in high-density railway networks, the first loop of the intelligent O&M system introduces a continuous general survey technology based on operational trains. A fundamental prerequisite for this technology is the utilization of vehicles operating under constant speed, constant load, and consistent operational states (referred to as "isostates"). These isostates minimize the non-linear uncertainties in vehicle-track coupled dynamics, providing a stable "baseline" for the long-term trend analysis of track health. This sensing enhancement is realized through a transition from isolated sensor measurements to a multi-dimensional, pervasive perception framework that integrates hierarchical vibration, inertial references, and acoustic signals.

The core of this architecture is the multi-level vibration sensing system, which utilizes the vehicle’s mechanical structure as a natural transducer. Different vehicle components exhibit distinct filtering characteristics that correlate with specific track irregularity wavelengths. Axle Box Acceleration is directly coupled with the wheel-rail interface, making it exceptionally sensitive to high-frequency impacts. It is the primary data source for diagnosing rail surface defects and short-wavelength irregularities, such as squats, insulated joint failures, and rail corrugation(Molodova, Li and Dollevoet, 2011; Salvador et al., 2016) . However, the extreme vibration environment of the axle box often introduces high-frequency noise and integration drift, which can obscure geometric trends(Real Herráiz et al., 2012). To bridge this gap, bogie and car body accelerations are integrated into the system. While the primary and secondary suspension systems filter out high-frequency content, these sensors provide high-fidelity data for medium-to-long wavelength irregularities . Such data is critical for monitoring large-scale infrastructure changes, including subgrade settlement, bridge pier tilt, and slab track deformation(Li et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021) .
