To further enhance the precision of spatial trajectory reconstruction, Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) are incorporated to provide high-precision angular velocity data (e.g., pitch, roll, and yaw rates). Pure acceleration-based methods often suffer from signal-to-noise ratio degradation at low frequencies or during low-speed operations. The introduction of gyroscopic sensors allows for the compensation of these low-frequency errors. For instance, the bogie yaw rate has been demonstrated to be significantly more robust than lateral acceleration for estimating track alignment and gauge-related irregularities when the train operates at velocities as low as 10 m/s (Weston et al., 2007). By applying complementary filtering or Kalman filtering to fuse acceleration and angular velocity, the sensing system can accurately decouple the vehicle's attitude from the track's true geometry, enabling a precise mapping of the "absolute" track profile across a broad spectrum of wavelengths (Escalona, 2016).

Lastly, the fusion of acoustic sensing adds a non-contact diagnostic dimension to the general survey. Acoustic signals, such as wheel-rail interaction noise and interior carriage noise, possess extremely high sampling rates, allowing for the identification of micro-scale surface degradations that may not yet have triggered significant vibration responses. Advanced signal processing techniques, such as wavelet packet energy analysis and 1D-CNN-based feature extraction, have enabled the quantification of rail corrugation and wheel flats with high accuracy (Wei et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022). This synergy of multi-level vibration, inertial navigation, and acoustic perception creates a robust, "all-weather" sensing layer, ensuring that the continuous general survey can provide comprehensive and reliable track state information for subsequent AI-driven assessment.
Data Imputation and Enhancement

Within the framework of continuous general survey technology based on on-board vibration-noise sensing, the efficacy of downstream diagnostic models is fundamentally bottlenecked by raw data quality. Despite the deployment of advanced sensor networks across large-scale railway infrastructures, continuous signal acquisition is inevitably compromised by harsh dynamic environments, transient communication latencies, and sensor degradation. This disruption leads to highly fragmented and intrinsically imbalanced datasets. Consequently, establishing a robust data preprocessing pipeline is a critical prerequisite for reliable intelligent operation and maintenance (O&M). This pipeline specifically encompasses data imputation to rectify missing sensor observations and data enhancement to amplify rare fault signatures. The evolution of these methodologies reflects a continuous drive to capture the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of railway systems.

Under Missing Completely at Random (MCAR) or Missing at Random (MAR) assumptions, early data imputation typically relied on simple mean substitution or linear interpolation. To mitigate the bias of these univariate methods, multivariate statistical frameworks like Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) (Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011) were widely adopted. In transportation domains, foundational machine learning algorithms have demonstrated significant efficacy; for instance, Probabilistic Principal Component Analysis (PPCA) effectively recovers missing traffic flow data by extracting linear feature correlations (Qu et al., 2009). Additionally, the non-parametric MissForest algorithm (Stekhoven and Bühlmann, 2012) excels in handling mixed-type data without strict distributional assumptions. However, these fundamental approaches inherently rely on linear or local proximity assumptions, rendering them inadequate for capturing the highly non-linear, multidimensional dependencies within complex railway sensor networks.

To address these multidimensional dependencies, matrix factorization initially emerged to reconstruct missing values by extracting latent low-rank structures from highly sparse datasets(Koren, Bell and Volinsky, 2009). Because intelligent transportation data naturally encompass complex spatiotemporal dimensions—such as spatial nodes, time intervals, and sensor features—they inherently form multidimensional tensors rather than two-dimensional matrices. Consequently, low-rank tensor factorization extends this paradigm to preserve global topological properties across multiple modes, effectively capturing multi-way correlations for missing traffic volume imputation(Giancarlo, 2018). Nevertheless, their reliance on static rank assumptions restricts their adaptability to highly non-linear spatiotemporal shifts.

To capture such complex non-linear dynamics, deep recurrent and graph-based architectures have superseded static factorization models. Bidirectional recurrent neural networks directly learn missing values within the sequence graph, effectively modeling temporal decay and dynamic missing patterns in time series(Cao et al., 2018). Concurrently, inductive graph neural networks have advanced spatial-temporal kriging by leveraging the complex topological structures of transportation networks to infer data at unobserved spatial nodes(Wu et al., 2020). Despite their strong predictive capabilities, these models inherently rely on discrete time steps. This discrete nature poses significant challenges when addressing the irregularly sampled or continuously missing high-speed railway sensor signals, demanding a shift from discrete models to continuous-time dynamics.

To overcome the constraints of discrete time steps, Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs) offer a paradigm shift by modeling latent states as continuous-time dynamics. This continuous formulation is particularly adept at handling irregularly sampled data caused by transient communication failures in high-speed railways. Latent ODEs pioneered this approach by naturally interpolating missing values without requiring artificial time alignment(Rubanova, Chen and Duvenaud, 2019). Furthermore, Neural Controlled Differential Equations (NCDEs) extended this capability to process continuous incoming data streams (Kidger et al., 2020). In intelligent transportation, integrating continuous temporal CDEs with spatial graph networks has successfully resolved irregular traffic sensor failures(Choi et al., 2021). While highly effective for continuous temporal modeling, these dynamic systems do not explicitly capture the complex, underlying probability distributions of missing values, necessitating the introduction of deep generative frameworks.

To explicitly capture these complex underlying probability distributions, deep generative frameworks—most notably Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)—have been widely adopted. Unlike deterministic systems, generative approaches reconstruct missing values by learning the non-linear data distribution within a latent space. The pioneering Generative Adversarial Imputation Nets (GAIN) introduced an adversarial mechanism where a generator imputes missing components while a discriminator distinguishes them from observed data(Yoon, Jordon and Schaar, 2018). Within railway condition monitoring, customized GAN architectures have been successfully deployed to recover missing multi-sensor data from rolling stock and mechanical bearings, significantly enhancing diagnostic reliability(X. Wang et al., 2025). However, GAN-based imputation frequently suffers from training instability and mode collapse, highlighting the critical need for more stable and tractable probabilistic generative paradigms.

To address the instability of adversarial training, diffusion models have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art probabilistic paradigm for data imputation. By defining a forward noise-injection process and learning a parameterized reverse denoising trajectory, these models offer highly stable and tractable generation. Conditional Score-based Diffusion Models (CSDI) pioneered this approach by probabilistically imputing time-series data through a conditional denoising mechanism(Tashiro et al., 2021). This process is particularly advantageous for complex, high-dimensional transportation networks. Recently, conditional diffusion frameworks have been tailored to reconstruct missing continuous multi-sensor signals in high-speed trains, demonstrating superior distributional fidelity compared to previous baselines(Yang et al., 2025). While these advanced imputation techniques successfully restore data completeness, the inherent scarcity of critical fault samples in real-world railway operations necessitates the complementary integration of data enhancement strategies.

While high-fidelity data imputation is critical for restoring the continuity of sensor networks, data enhancement is equally indispensable for the intelligent operation and maintenance of large-scale railway infrastructures. Imputation methodologies primarily address the random missingness of observations but cannot overcome the inherent scarcity and severe class imbalance of critical fault events. In real-world railway operations, anomalous conditions occur infrequently, resulting in a pronounced long-tail distribution. Therefore, generating synthetic fault samples to enrich the minority feature space is essential for training robust diagnostic models.To mitigate this extreme class imbalance, heuristic resampling techniques were initially adopted. Instead of merely duplicating rare samples, the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) generates synthetic instances by interpolating along feature-space line segments joining nearest neighbors(Chawla et al., 2002). Subsequently, the Adaptive Synthetic (ADASYN) approach dynamically generates more data for harder-to-learn minority examples, adaptively shifting the decision boundary(He et al., 2008). In railway engineering, these interpolation techniques are widely utilized; for instance, modified SMOTE algorithms have successfully balanced sparse defect datasets to improve the fault diagnosis of railway turnout systems(Li et al., 2022). Nevertheless, when applied to the highly non-linear fault boundaries of complex railway components, these linear strategies often introduce noisy synthetic artifacts, necessitating the shift towards more sophisticated signal-level transformations.

To overcome linear interpolation artifacts, signal-level transformations and feature mixing strategies directly manipulate continuous time-series data to simulate diverse operating conditions. Techniques such as adding Gaussian noise or time-stretching physically alter original sensor signals, while the mix-up approach improves model generalization by interpolating both features and labels to smooth decision boundaries(Zhang et al., 2018). Within railway condition monitoring, these model-independent augmentations have proven highly effective for diagnosing faults in critical rotating machinery under variable dynamic loads(Lyu et al., 2022). Nevertheless, because signal warping and feature mixing primarily recombine existing observations rather than generating entirely new, high-fidelity fault distributions, capturing the highly complex non-linearities of rare railway defects necessitates a transition to advanced deep generative modeling.

To synthesize entirely new, high-fidelity fault distributions, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have become the cornerstone of advanced data enhancement. By optimizing an adversarial mechanism, conditional GANs, such as CTGAN, effectively model non-Gaussian and discrete data without relying on prior structural assumptions(Xu et al., 2019). In railway engineering, customized GANs are increasingly deployed to synthesize realistic samples of extreme minority classes, specifically generating artificial railway track irregularities to augment sparse diagnostic datasets(Bobadilla and Martin, 2024). However, while standard GANs excel given moderate sample sizes, they frequently suffer from mode collapse and degraded feature boundaries when trained under extremely limited data regimes, driving the adoption of contrastive learning and diffusion models.

To overcome mode collapse in extremely limited data regimes, contrastive learning and diffusion architectures have been introduced to stabilize feature synthesis. Contrastive learning enhances generative networks by explicitly maximizing latent distances between distinct classes, thereby sharpening decision boundaries. In railway applications, contrastive GANs have successfully synthesized rare rail surface defects, preventing training instability when real samples are exceptionally scarce(Du, Gao and Li, 2023). Concurrently, diffusion models have transitioned from data imputation to augmentation. Frameworks such as TabDDPM (Kotelnikov et al., 2024) synthesize high-fidelity structural data through stable iterative denoising, outperforming standard GANs with minimal prior observations. Nevertheless, applying these highly complex probabilistic models directly to extensive, multivariate railway sensor signals necessitates their integration with advanced sequential representation architectures.

To effectively process extensive, multivariate sensor sequences, Transformer-based architectures have redefined data enhancement paradigms. By leveraging self-attention mechanisms, Transformers capture long-range temporal dependencies without relying on localized receptive fields. To enhance sequence representations under limited supervision, frameworks have been designed to intentionally mask and reconstruct segments of multivariate time series, thereby extracting robust generalized features(Zerveas et al., 2020). In intelligent railway operation and maintenance, this paradigm elegantly addresses severe fault sample shortages. Notably, recent approaches integrating Convolutional Transformers with pseudo-synthetic data generation algorithms have significantly improved the fault diagnosis accuracy of complex railway turnout systems(Fu et al., 2024). Ultimately, these attention-driven enhancement strategies provide the requisite high-dimensional feature fidelity to support robust, large-scale predictive maintenance.

In summary, the evolution of data imputation and enhancement strategies provides a comprehensive solution to the inherent data imperfections of on-board vibration-noise sensing systems. The progression from foundational statistical interpolations to state-of-the-art continuous dynamics and generative architectures ensures the extraction of high-fidelity, balanced feature spaces from chaotic sensor streams. By strictly reconstructing missing temporal dynamics and artificially synthesizing minority fault representations, these advanced methodologies bridge the critical gap between raw hardware perception and actionable intelligence. Ultimately, this stabilized and enriched data foundation paves the way for the subsequent deployment of advanced AI-based inverse mapping models and large-scale assessment frameworks in railway predictive maintenance.

blocks.text: AI-Based Inverse Mapping Model

The fundamental operating premise of on-board vibration and noise sensing systems is, in essence, an inverse problem. The physical forward process—from track geometric irregularities and structural defects to the vehicle’s dynamic response—can be approximately described by a vehicle-track coupled dynamic model; however, the inverse path—reconstructing track conditions from measured vibration and acoustic signals—is inherently ill-defined. The one-to-many nature of this mapping implies that, under different operating speeds, vehicle states, and environmental conditions, various combinations of track defects may produce nearly identical onboard response characteristics. Traditional physics-based inverse analysis strategies (such as iterative finite element model refinement) are extremely computationally expensive at the scale of a continuous network-wide survey, and are highly sensitive to modeling uncertainties. The maturity of deep learning has opened up a fundamentally different path: AI-based inverse mapping models directly learn the complex nonlinear mapping relationships between sensor observations and track conditions from the data, replacing explicit physical inversion with statistical surrogate models, resulting in an inference cost that is virtually negligible. Such models have now become an indispensable algorithmic bridge between the raw outputs of onboard sensor systems and the actionable track condition information required for intelligent operations and maintenance.

The core challenge in realizing the full diagnostic potential of on-board vibration and noise sensing systems lies not only in accurate signal processing but also in solving an inherently ill-posed inverse problem: reconstructing the spatially distributed mechanical state of the track from the integrated, coupled dynamic response measured at the vehicle body. The physical forward process is well characterized: track geometric irregularities, local stiffness deficiencies, and rail surface defects each excite characteristic dynamic modes in the vehicle-track coupled system, and their effects can be measured at multiple locations on the vehicle in the form of acceleration, velocity, or acoustic signatures. However, the challenge in the inverse direction is far more daunting. The observed vehicle body response is the result of complex convolution of multiple track excitation sources, filtered through the frequency-selective dynamics of the vehicle suspension and wheel-axle system, and further disturbed by wheel out-of-roundness, aerodynamic loads, and measurement noise. Consequently, under different operating speeds and vehicle configurations, various combinations of track defects may produce nearly identical on-board signatures, rendering the mapping relationship inherently non-unique. Classic physics-based inversion strategies (such as iterative finite element model refinement or Kalman filter-based state estimation) are either computationally prohibitively expensive at the scale of a full-network continuous survey or require idealized linear structural assumptions—assumptions that are difficult to justify in the presence of contact nonlinearities and spatially heterogeneous track characteristics. These limitations form the core motivation for AI-based inverse mapping: learning effective inverse operators directly from data without requiring explicit analytical forms—since the underlying physics itself cannot provide such forms.

Previous AI-based inverse mapping methods have established a rich set of learnable solutions for this problem. For example, end-to-end deep neural networks that map vehicle body acceleration to track mass index (Ma et al., 2019), multi-scale convolutional architectures for defect classification (Acikgoz and Korkmaz, 2023; Y. Wang et al., 2025), and multi-task frameworks for jointly estimating track parameters (C. Li et al., 2024; Pu et al., 2024) collectively demonstrate that the wheel-rail–vehicle dynamic transfer chain encodes track state information sufficient to support data-driven inversion. However, the gap between laboratory-scale proof-of-concept and full-network operational deployment remains vast, and bridging this gap requires a fundamental reevaluation of how inverse mapping models are designed, trained, and validated.

At the same time, the most significant structural limitation of the current generation of inverse mapping models is their implicit assumption of stationarity. Every supervised learning model implicitly encodes a prior distribution regarding the joint distribution of input signals and output track states observed during training. When a model trained on summer data from flat terrain is deployed on a winter mountain slope line, the mechanics of wheel-rail contact, the thermal behavior of ballast, and the aerodynamic load spectrum will all shift simultaneously—and the trained mapping model will confuse track conditions with these operational effects, losing calibration accuracy in a systematic manner that is difficult to detect in the absence of ground truth. This issue is not marginal but fundamental: the entire value proposition of on-board continuous sensing hinges on the ability of models calibrated during dedicated measurement periods to generalize to daily passenger operations under all conditions.

A promising research direction to address this challenge lies in domain-adversarial training frameworks, which explicitly decouple track-state-dependent features from operational-condition-dependent confounding factors, training models to generate representations capable of predicting track states while maintaining invariance to speed, vehicle load, and seasonal factors. Complementing this, meta-learning approaches—which train models on a task distribution rather than a single task—offer the potential for rapid, low-data-requirement adaptation to new operational conditions or previously unencountered track geometries, thereby significantly reducing the need for re-calibration data when deploying models to new network segments. The construction of standardized, cross-network benchmark datasets capable of capturing the full diversity of operational conditions across multiple railway systems will serve as an indispensable foundational project for advancing and fairly evaluating the aforementioned adaptive strategies.

Equally critical and equally unresolved is the fact that virtually all deployed inverse mapping systems lack quantification of uncertainty. Current models provide only point estimates without confidence intervals—whether for predicted track quality indices, classified defect types, or reconstructed stiffness fields—and thus offer no basis for maintenance decision-makers to distinguish between high-confidence diagnostic conclusions and unreliable extrapolations for out-of-distribution inputs. This is unacceptable in safety-critical infrastructure scenarios: tamping operations triggered by overconfident, degraded predictions waste maintenance budgets and disrupt traffic; while sections of the road misclassified as healthy due to false confidence pose safety hazards. The field must advance toward probabilistic inverse mapping, incorporating a posterior distribution with each output to honestly characterize aleatory uncertainty—irreducible noise in sensor observations—and epistemic uncertainty—the model’s lack of knowledge in regions of the input space where training data coverage is insufficient. Deep ensemble learning, Monte Carlo Dropout, Bayesian neural networks, and conformal prediction all offer viable approximations to this ideal, each presenting different trade-offs between calibration quality, computational cost, and deployment complexity. Among these, conformal prediction is particularly attractive for operational deployment because it provides guarantees of coverage with limited samples without requiring distribution assumptions, enabling maintenance engineers to use prediction intervals that are statistically valid regardless of the underlying model architecture. Integrating uncertainty-aware outputs into the decision-making layer—where the predicted state distribution is propagated through a risk model to generate maintenance recommendations with explicit confidence levels—represents a decisive leap from AI-based diagnostic tools to AI-based decision support systems.

PINN offers a structurally distinct and theoretically grounded approach to simultaneously address the aforementioned challenges. By directly embedding the partial differential equations governing track-structure dynamicsinto the training loss as physical residual terms (Ding et al., 2024; Q. Wang et al., 2024), PINNs impose continuous structural consistency constraints across the entire spatio-temporal domain rather than merely at discrete training points. In the inverse configuration, unknown physical parameters—such as foundation stiffness distribution, ballast damping coefficients, or local damage indices—are treated as additional trainable variables and recovered in tandem with the response field by minimizing a data-physical joint loss.

This framework possesses several properties directly relevant to operations: physical residuals serve as a powerful regularization mechanism under sparse sensor conditions, enabling reliable parameter identification from data with a measurement density far lower than that required by purely data-driven methods; the recovered parameters can be interpreted directly as physical quantities rather than abstract latent variables; physical constraints implicitly encode prior knowledge about structural behavior, partially mitigating distribution shifts by anchoring the model to physical laws that hold regardless of operational conditions (Haghighat et al., 2021; Xu and Darve, 2021).

Despite these advantages, the application of PINN to large-scale railway inverse problems remains in its infancy and faces non-trivial obstacles. A significant challenge that cannot be overlooked is that the contact mechanics at the wheel-rail interface exhibit strong nonlinearity, velocity dependence, and spatial randomness, making it difficult to express them in a compact PDE form. The spatial non-stationarity of real-world track characteristics at scales far smaller than standard measurement segment lengths makes it difficult to justify the assumption of a smoothly parameterized PDE domain. The computational cost of evaluating higher-order spatial and temporal derivatives via automatic differentiation on large-scale rail network length datasets remains a practical obstacle to deployment. A promising research frontier lies in hierarchical hybrid architectures: a PINN component constrains the dynamic response at the single-sleeper-spacing scale, where physical mechanisms are well-understood, coupled with a data-driven component that learns effective large-scale spatial statistical patterns of stiffness and damage distribution from historical network-wide records. In this architecture, physical constraints are no longer universal hard constraints but rather scale-specific regularization mechanisms—most stringent where the physical model is most accurate, and most lenient where data-driven learning can compensate for modeling uncertainties.

blocks.text: Looking to the long-term future, the most transformative advancement will be the emergence of spatially consistent, network-wide inverse mapping—a fundamental leap from estimating the state of isolated track segments to maintaining a continuously updated, physically consistent dynamic model of the entire railway network. No matter how accurate a single-segment model may be, it is structurally incapable of capturing phenomena that inherently belong to the network level: the spatial propagation of ballast degradation fronts from high-stress locations to adjacent sections; the load redistribution effect where local stiffness defects transfer excess dynamic loads to neighboring track units; or the systematic interaction patterns between adjacent maintenance interventions, where tamping at one location may shift the degradation gradient to an adjacent untreated section. Network-wide inverse mapping requires an architecture natively operating on a graph representation of the railway network, where nodes represent track sections or discrete infrastructure units, and edges encode physical coupling relationships and spatial adjacencies. Graph neural networks—trained to propagate physical constraints and uncertainty estimates between spatially connected nodes while assimilating heterogeneous data streams (records from periodic inspection train passes, continuous IoT sensor data, maintenance event logs, and historical weather and load data)— —provides a natural computational foundation for this network state estimation problem. The integration of a digital twin framework—with a continuously updated railway computational model serving as a dynamic prior for inversion—further enhances the physical consistency of the reconstructed state and supports prospective simulation of the consequences of candidate maintenance interventions prior to their implementation. This convergence of physically constrained deep learning, spatio-temporal graph neural networks, Bayesian state estimation, and digital twin infrastructure defines the long-term research frontier toward which current AI-based inverse mapping advancements are gradually converging, and represents the direction in which the field should deliberately direct its methodological investments.
Assessment Technology Based on AI Large Models

With the continuous expansion of high-speed railway, urban rail transit, and heavy-haul railway networks, railway systems are gradually shifting from traditional experience-driven maintenance management toward data-driven, knowledge-driven, and intelligent decision-making paradigms. Railway operation and maintenance scenarios are characterized by complex equipment types, variable operating environments, strict safety constraints, and severe consequences of failures. These scenarios involve multiple subsystems, including rolling stock, track structures, turnouts, signalling systems, communication systems, catenary systems, bridges, tunnels, slopes, and dispatching control. During long-term operation, railway systems accumulate large amounts of multi-source heterogeneous data, including sensor monitoring data, inspection images and videos, equipment maintenance records, fault reports, accident reports, regulations, standards, dispatching logs, and emergency response documents. These data include not only structured time-series information but also a large amount of unstructured text, image, and multimodal information. Therefore, how to effectively organize, understand, extract knowledge from, and transform these data into maintenance and safety decisions has become an important issue in railway intelligent operation and maintenance. Large language models have strong natural language understanding, contextual reasoning, and human-computer interaction capabilities, providing new methods for railway professional text processing and fault diagnosis. Peng (Peng et al., 2025) proposed RFD-LLM, a large language model for fault diagnosis of railway vehicle onboard controllers. For high-speed train equipment diagnosis, Zhang (Z. Zhang et al., 2025) proposed “Bogie Doctor”, which uses deep learning to analyze high-speed train maintenance logs and realize automated fault diagnosis of bogies. Miao (Miao, Wu and Zhang, 2025) further combined knowledge graphs with large language models and proposed a Graph RAG-based method for train bogie fault diagnosis. Chen (Chen et al., 2025) developed an intelligent question-answering system for railway locomotive maintenance standardization, using large language models to retrieve and answer questions related to maintenance standards, operating procedures, and regulatory clauses. Li et al. proposed an intelligent human-computer interactive training assistant system for rail systems to improve the efficiency of railway personnel training and knowledge acquisition (Li et al., 2025). These studies show that large language models can be used not only for fault diagnosis but also for railway knowledge services, personnel training, and standardized operation assistance.

Although general-purpose large language models have strong language generation capabilities, they may suffer from knowledge gaps, inconsistency with railway regulations, and hallucinations in professional railway scenarios. To improve the reliability of model outputs, retrieval-augmented generation and knowledge graphs have become important supporting technologies for railway large model applications. Zheng (W. Zheng et al., 2026) proposed CARAG, a context-aware retrieval-augmented generation framework for railway operation and maintenance question answering. The framework introduces a spatial knowledge graph to represent spatial relationships among railway lines, equipment, and maintenance objects. Wang (Wang et al., 2026) proposed an instruction fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation framework for intelligent defect diagnosis and maintenance decision support in high-speed railway turnouts. Wang (Wang Xianghao et al., 2026) also proposed an intelligent generation method for railway emergency response strategies based on knowledge retrieval enhancement, combining emergency response knowledge with generative models to assist in generating railway emergency handling plans. Knowledge graphs have also been widely used for knowledge acquisition and dynamic updating in low-annotation railway scenarios. Cai (Cai et al., 2026) proposed a unified LLM-KG framework for low-annotation urban rail transit signal system operation, focusing on knowledge acquisition and dynamic updating.

Tang (Tang et al., 2026) proposed LoFT-CLIP, a few-shot anomaly detection method for railway fasteners based on large vision-language models, which alleviates the problem of insufficient abnormal fastener samples. Zhan (Zhan, Wu and Ma, 2025) investigated the optimization of large railway vision models for efficient in-context learning, aiming to improve model adaptability and inference efficiency in railway inspection tasks. Zheng (X. Zheng et al., 2026) proposed a generation-based defect detection system for rail transit infrastructure, and further studied a railway side slope hazard detection system based on generative models. For visual diagnosis of rolling stock systems, Zhang (Zhang, Wang and You, 2025) proposed GFIA, which applies vision-language models to fault image analysis of train bogie transmission systems, realizing semantic description and diagnostic interpretation of fault images. Chen (Chen Yong, An Zhuoaobo, and Zhou Jianyu, 2025) proposed a semantic description method for high-speed railway catenary insulator defects based on diffusion model detection. These studies show that multimodal models can transform image detection results into more interpretable semantic information, thereby improving the explainability of inspection results and the efficiency of human-machine collaboration.

In addition to static defect detection, railway operational safety also requires real-time perception of dynamic scenarios. Huang(Huang and Deng, 2025) proposed a method that combines multi-agent cooperative large language models with an edge stream processing engine for real-time tracking of railway intruders]. Kang (Kang, Yang and Choi, 2026) proposed RAISA, a vision-based intelligent safety guidance agent for railway operations using modular prompt-orchestrated reasoning. Wang (Wang, 2025) proposed HTFN, a hybrid deep reinforcement learning framework for UAV-based railway inspection with DeepSeek integration, aiming to improve the decision-making capability of UAV inspection tasks.

Railway maintenance tasks show strong spatiotemporal coupling characteristics and are influenced by historical operation data, weather, holidays, urban activities, network structure, and unexpected events. In dispatching and risk control, Zhao (Zhao and Liu, 2025) proposed a high-speed train operational risk prevention and control model based on a large language model.

Railway safety management relies heavily on accident reports, fault reports, regulatory standards, and test cases. Traditional text analysis methods often depend on manual annotation and keyword matching, making it difficult to fully mine the deep relationships among accident causes, risk factors, and human error mechanisms. In recent years, language models have gradually been applied to railway safety text analysis and regulation-related testing tasks. Hong (Hong, Clifton and Nelson, 2024) proposed a data-driven conceptual framework for understanding the nature of hazards in railway accidents. Irshad and Walsh (Irshad and Walsh, 2026) used language models to learn from aviation and railway accident reports, focusing on human errors and error mechanisms. Li and Zeng (Li and Zeng, 2026) extracted and analyzed causative words from metro safety event texts, helping identify key causal factors in safety events. These studies show that language models can extract risk factors from large amounts of accident and safety event texts and assist safety managers in experience summarization and risk warning.

Predictive maintenance is an important component of railway intelligent operation and maintenance. Its core objective is to formulate appropriate maintenance strategies before failures occur based on equipment condition and degradation trends. With the development of multi-source data and artificial intelligence, railway predictive maintenance is moving toward multimodal perception, streaming data analysis, and explainable decision-making. Garcia-Mendez (Garcia-Mendez et al., 2025) proposed an explainable machine learning framework for railway predictive maintenance using data streams from the metro operator of Portugal, emphasizing model explainability and engineering applicability in actual operational data streams. Siahkouhi (Siahkouhi et al., 2026) studied AI-assisted fibre optic sensing frameworks for automated monitoring of railway infrastructure, demonstrating the potential of distributed fibre optic sensing and intelligent analysis in railway infrastructure condition monitoring. Martinez (Martinez et al., 2025) systematically reviewed the application of physics-informed neural networks in structural analysis and monitoring of railway bridges, showing that combining physical constraints with data-driven models is an important direction for improving model reliability. Kang (Kang et al., 2026) proposed an attention-based multimodal anomaly detection method for high-speed train control systems, integrating multi-source signals for control system anomaly identification.

The Second Closed Loop: Precision Maintenance and Verified Intervention

The second closed loop should be understood as a precision-maintenance loop rather than as a general robotics loop. In the proposed dual-loop architecture(Figure 2), the first loop supplies broad coverage: it observes long mileage, detects abnormal state evolution, ranks risk, and identifies candidate work sites. The second loop is activated only after such a candidate has been identified. Its purpose is not to inspect the whole network again, but to transform a warning into a local repair target, execute an intervention with controllable parameters, and verify the effect through remeasurement. This is the conceptual shift from “knowing that a section is deteriorating” to “knowing exactly what to repair, how to repair it, and whether the repair has changed the state as expected.”

This definition also clarifies why the second loop should be evaluated differently from the first. The first loop is judged by coverage, frequency, sensitivity to state evolution, false-alarm control, and economic scalability. The second loop is judged by localization accuracy, diagnostic confidence, repair-boundary definition, parameter controllability, safety assurance, and measured repair effectiveness. A second-loop system that only adds high-resolution inspection is incomplete, because it does not close the maintenance action. Likewise, an autonomous machine that can perform a repair but cannot verify the resulting state is only an automated tool, not a closed-loop maintenance system. The defining property of the second loop is verified intervention.

The planning view behind this loop is therefore deliberately engineering-oriented. It does not assume that general-purpose embodied intelligence can immediately replace railway maintenance crews. Instead, it treats intelligence as a layered capability embedded into a conservative safety regime. The lower layer provides precision localization, high-resolution measurement and tool feedback. The middle layer converts local state into repair parameters and acceptance criteria. The upper layer preserves human authorization, rule traceability and maintenance accountability. This arrangement is compatible with the railway context, where local autonomy is useful only when it remains auditable and recoverable under possession-window, traffic-safety and asset-management constraints.

Four design principles follow. First, the loop must be target-specific: each task should define its own measurable state, action variable and acceptance criterion. Second, the loop must be coordinate-consistent: pre-repair measurement, execution and post-repair verification must refer to the same mileage and asset object. Third, the loop must be effect-oriented: success should be judged by state change and durability, not merely by work completion. Fourth, the loop must be incrementally deployable: early systems should focus on bounded tasks such as rail-profile correction, fastener intervention, local geometry restoration or ballast-condition verification before moving toward broader autonomous repair.
From network alert to repairable engineering object

The first step of the second loop is to convert a network-level alert into a repairable engineering object. A first-loop model may detect abnormal vibration, noise, track geometry, rail corrugation, stiffness variation, fastener anomaly or state-evolution rate over a relatively broad interval. Such an output is valuable for screening, but it is not yet a repair instruction. A repair instruction requires a much tighter definition: the target asset, the mileage position, the defect boundary, the dominant mechanism, the intervention type, the action parameters and the acceptance test. The second loop therefore begins at the point where condition monitoring becomes repair specification.

This conversion requires spatial precision. A maintenance site must be mapped to a mileage coordinate, track, rail side or component identity. For linear assets, even a small coordinate mismatch can lead to ineffective repair or misleading verification. A geometry dip may have a boundary of only tens of metres; a corrugation problem may vary by wavelength band and rail side; a loose-fastener cluster may be discontinuous; a slab-support problem may be invisible on the surface but associated with a narrow support zone. The system must therefore express the defect not as an abstract risk score but as a geometric and component-level object that can be revisited.

The conversion also requires diagnostic precision. Many railway defects are symptoms of deeper mechanisms. A local irregularity may result from ballast fouling, drainage failure, hanging sleepers, transition-zone stiffness mismatch, subgrade frost heave or slab-interface voiding. Repeatedly correcting the visible geometry without addressing the cause may improve short-term measurement values while increasing long-term recurrence. In the second loop, the target object should therefore include a causal hypothesis. The hypothesis need not be perfect, but it must be explicit enough to guide the choice between tamping, grinding, cleaning, tightening, replacement, grouting, drainage improvement or structural reinforcement.

Finally, the conversion requires action precision. A repair category is not sufficient. Tamping requires lift and lining values; grinding requires depth, pass pattern and profile target; fastener intervention requires torque or replacement criteria; ballast cleaning requires depth and boundary; slab repair requires injection or local structural treatment parameters. The second loop becomes meaningful only when the system can connect the measured state to such controllable action variables. This is the main difference between precision maintenance and enhanced diagnosis.
Precision measurement and local state representation

Precision measurement is the local state factory of the second loop. It differs from the screening function of the first loop in scale, purpose and tolerance. Screening seeks high coverage and low marginal cost; precision measurement seeks repeatability, calibration and actionability. Its product should be a compact local state representation that a decision module, machine operator or robot can use directly. For railway line maintenance, this representation may include local geometry amplitude, spatial frequency, rail-profile deviation, corrugation depth, fastener status, ballast or support indicator, environmental condition, track-side identity, uncertainty and historical recurrence. The key requirement is that the state vector should be both physically meaningful and executable.

A practical second-loop measurement system should combine three levels. The first is high-resolution surface measurement, including track geometry, rail profile, corrugation, surface defect and component-position sensing. This level defines the visible target and the required boundary of action. The second is support-condition or subsurface diagnosis, such as ballast fouling, voids, moisture or weak support zones. This level helps distinguish symptoms from causes. The third is dynamic or contextual measurement, including acceleration, strain, temperature, axle-load context and local response under operating conditions. This level is especially important at transition zones, where measured geometry alone may underestimate the mechanism that causes repeated deterioration.

The central algorithmic problem is not only feature extraction but mileage alignment. The same target must be recoverable across the first-loop alert, local precision measurement, tool execution and post-repair remeasurement. This requires fusion of odometry, inertial sensing, GNSS or BeiDou when available, known track features, digital track maps, signal matching and machine-specific offsets. The issue is often treated as a preprocessing step, but in precision maintenance it is a core safety function. If before-after data cannot be proven to refer to the same object, the system cannot claim that the intervention changed the state.

The local state representation should also include uncertainty. Railway maintenance is performed under time pressure, outdoor conditions and imperfect measurement. A precise-looking number without uncertainty can be misleading. For example, a predicted corrugation depth, ballast fouling index or slab-support anomaly should be accompanied by a confidence measure, data-source trace and recommended confirmation method. This makes the system more robust in deployment because it can distinguish between cases suitable for automatic action, cases requiring human confirmation, and cases requiring additional measurement before repair.
Real-time decision-making and controllable intervention

The decision module of the second loop should be local, real-time and intervention-oriented. Its role is not to generate an annual maintenance plan; that remains the task of the maintenance-management system and the first loop. The second-loop decision module answers immediate questions: what is the dominant maintenance object, what action should be taken, what parameters should be used, what risk should be controlled during execution, and what measured result will count as successful repair. This decision is narrower than network optimization but technically more demanding because it is tied to a physical operation.

A robust local decision should combine four sources of reasoning. Standards and management rules define the safety envelope and acceptance thresholds. Expert rules encode the causal knowledge of track engineers, such as when repeated tamping is unlikely to solve a transition-zone problem. Predictive models estimate recurrence and intervention durability. Local measurement provides the immediate state and action boundary. The result should not be a black-box command. It should be an auditable recommendation that includes the state evidence, confidence level, selected action, process parameters, acceptance criterion and fallback action. In safety-critical contexts, the system should be allowed to recommend human review instead of forced autonomy.

The action model should be expressed as a state-action-effect tuple. The state contains the local features and their uncertainty; the action contains the repair type and process parameters; the effect contains the target before-after change and the expected durability. This tuple is useful for two reasons. Operationally, it tells the machine or crew what to do and how to verify it. Scientifically, it creates a rare but valuable dataset: pre-repair state, executed action, process log, post-repair state and later recurrence. Such paired intervention data are more useful for future learning than isolated inspection data because they record how the infrastructure responds to maintenance.

Controllable intervention requires process feedback. For grinding, this may include actual removal depth, post-profile error and thermal or surface-quality constraints. For tamping, it may include lift, lining, compaction and residual geometry deviation. For fastener work, it may include target localization, torque, tool angle and visual confirmation. For ballast or slab support treatment, it may include injected volume, pressure response, subsurface change and local geometry recovery. The common requirement is that the machine should not only receive a command; it should report what was actually delivered. This delivery record is the bridge between decision and verification.

The second loop also changes the meaning of optimization. In conventional planning, optimization often means minimizing cost, possession time or expected risk at the network level. In precision maintenance, optimization is local and effect-based: choose the smallest safe intervention that changes the state sufficiently and durably. This principle is important because over-intervention may waste possession time and damage materials, while under-intervention may produce rapid recurrence. The second loop should therefore learn not only where to intervene, but also how much intervention is enough.
Robotic execution, verification feedback and deployment roadmap

Robotic execution is a necessary enabler for the mature second loop, but it should not dominate the concept. The immediate goal is not a fully general railway repair robot. The credible path is task-constrained automation: autonomous or remotely supervised mobility, high-precision localization, specialized sensing payloads, constrained tool modules, process monitoring, human authorization and post-work verification. Existing autonomous railway platforms already show that localization, obstacle detection, remote monitoring and modular payload integration can be achieved in railway environments (Li et al., 2024). These platforms can become carriers for second-loop measurement and intervention modules, provided that the repair task is well bounded and the safety case is explicit.

The same incremental logic applies to intervention tools. Fastener automation is a useful example because the target is discrete, the operation is bounded, and the endpoint can be measured by torque and visual confirmation. The rail-fastener installation robot developed by Guo combines visual recognition, bolt localization, manipulator feeding and electric-wrench fastening. The broader significance of such a system is not that it solves all maintenance tasks, but that it demonstrates the structure of a feasible precision-repair module: identify the component, localize the target, execute a controlled action, and verify the endpoint. Similar task-specific modules can be developed for rail grinding assistance, local profile correction, bolt and fastener inspection, small-part replacement, and targeted measurement after tamping or cleaning.

Embodied intelligence should therefore be introduced selectively. The useful capabilities are active perception, target reacquisition, force-aware control, tool-state monitoring and safe adaptive correction. A robot may reposition a sensor to reduce occlusion, remeasure after tool contact, adjust a trajectory, stop when force exceeds a safe envelope, or request human review when uncertainty is too high. These capabilities are consistent with the general embodied-intelligence view that perception, decision and action should be integrated in an interactive physical environment. For railway deployment, however, the autonomy must be constrained by engineering rules, tool limits, possession conditions and traceable safety logic.

Remeasurement is the closure condition of the second loop. After the intervention, the system must measure the same target again using the same coordinate reference or a calibrated equivalent. The remeasurement should answer four questions: was the target reached, did the state change as intended, does the residual state satisfy the acceptance criterion, and should another local correction be performed? This makes maintenance evidence-based at the action level. A conventional work record may show that a grinding, tamping or fastening job was completed. A closed-loop record shows the pre-repair state, the selected action, the delivered process parameters, the post-repair state and the decision about acceptance or rework.

A realistic deployment roadmap can be divided into four stages. The first stage is human-in-the-loop precision measurement, where candidate sites from the first loop are remeasured locally and converted into repairable objects. The second stage is decision support, where the system recommends action parameters and acceptance criteria while engineers retain approval authority. The third stage is semi-automated execution, where specialized machines or robots execute bounded operations under human supervision and report process data. The fourth stage is closed-loop learning, where repeated state-action-effect records are used to improve local decisions, quantify repair durability and update the first-loop state-evolution models. This roadmap avoids premature full autonomy while still moving decisively toward precise, auditable and self-improving maintenance.

In this sense, the second loop is the mechanism that turns state evolution into state control. The first loop tells the operator where the infrastructure is changing and where risk may accumulate. The second loop intervenes at selected sites, measures the local object in higher resolution, chooses a controllable action, verifies the effect and records the result. Over time, this architecture should reduce repeated symptom treatment, improve the traceability of maintenance decisions, and create a high-quality intervention dataset. Its value is not only automation; it is the ability to make railway maintenance more precise, explainable and learnable.
Case Studies
International Cases: Implementation Forms and Open Problems of the Dual-Loop Architecture

The domestic cases discussed above demonstrate how line-scale inspection, multi-source diagnosis and robotic equipment can be organized within an intelligent operation and maintenance (O&M) framework. International practice provides a complementary perspective. Rather than presenting a fully autonomous system in which every step has already been closed, recent international studies show that the constituent functions of the proposed dual-loop architecture have emerged at different spatial scales and levels of maturity. Corridor-scale distributed sensing, train-borne monitoring, asset-specific instrumentation, multi-source condition inference, predictive maintenance economics and feedback-oriented physical intervention have all been tested on operational railway lines or representative field assets. These cases are therefore reviewed here according to their roles in the O&M chain, rather than as isolated demonstrations of individual technologies.

From Periodic Inspection to Multi-Scale and Transferable Perception

The perception link of intelligent railway O&M is evolving along two complementary directions. The first is an increase in spatial and temporal coverage, represented by distributed sensing and train-borne monitoring. The second is an increase in asset specificity, represented by permanently instrumented switches and crossings. Together, these developments respond to the limitations of periodic inspection vehicles: although such vehicles provide accurate geometry measurements, they only observe the line at discrete times and cannot continuously capture rapid deterioration or short-lived abnormal events.

At the corridor scale, distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) converts an optical fiber into a spatially distributed vibration sensor. The review by Rahman et al. (2024) shows that railroad DAS research has expanded from train tracking and external-event detection toward structural health monitoring, defect detection and condition diagnosis. Its engineering significance lies in its ability to provide long-range and quasi-continuous measurements without installing a dense array of independent point sensors. Within the first loop, DAS can serve as a background perception layer that identifies abnormal sections and triggers higher-resolution inspection. This forms a hierarchical process in which continuous but indirect sensing is followed by targeted geometry measurement, ground-penetrating radar, local visual inspection or robotic examination.

The application boundary of DAS is equally important. Acoustic and vibration signatures depend on train type, speed, axle load, fiber location, cable-soil coupling and environmental noise. The technology therefore detects changes in the response field more readily than it identifies a unique structural cause. This distinction prevents continuous sensing from being equated with a completed diagnostic loop. Corridor-scale DAS is most valuable when used to prioritize reinspection and when its outputs are fused with asset, vehicle and maintenance databases.

Train-borne drive-by monitoring provides another route to increasing observation frequency because in-service or regularly operating vehicles can repeatedly sample the track. However, vibration features measured on one line often follow a different distribution on another line owing to changes in vehicle condition, speed, track form and operating environment. Ghiasi et al. (2025) addressed this problem through an unsupervised domain-adaptation framework for drive-by diagnosis of track geometry defects. A classifier constructed from a labelled source line was transferred to an unlabelled target line, and the framework was evaluated using field measurements from high-speed trains operating on four different lines across twelve domain-adaptation tasks. The study therefore moves beyond line-specific classification and directly addresses a practical obstacle to network-scale deployment: a model cannot realistically be relabelled and retrained from the beginning for every new line.
Figure The schematic of the proposed UDA framework for drive-by railway track monitoring(Ghiasi et al., 2025)

This case adds a necessary generalization layer to the perception-assessment loop. The objective is no longer only to collect more data, but to make knowledge learned from one operating domain usable in another. Domain adaptation partially reduces the distribution gap between lines, yet it does not remove the need for engineering validation. Changes in defect definitions, maintenance standards, sensor layouts and vehicle-track interaction can still produce incorrect transfer. Consequently, cross-line transfer should be combined with uncertainty estimation and a mechanism for requesting target-line labels when model confidence is insufficient.

At the asset scale, Milosevic et al. (2022) combined sleeper-mounted accelerometers, three-dimensional geometry scans and multi-body vehicle-track simulations for six in situ crossing panels. The proposed condition indicator was calculated from track responses in a wavelength-related frequency band and exhibited a strong relationship with simulated vertical wheel-rail contact force under different crossing and track conditions. This case is significant because it links a measurable dynamic response to a physically meaningful interaction quantity. It therefore provides more diagnostic value than an isolated acceleration threshold.

The measured-simulated comparison also exposes the limitations of the current implementation. The scanned crossing regions were shorter than the full dynamic interaction zone, and measured accelerations contained excitation sources not represented in the model, including long-wavelength irregularities, wheel out-of-roundness and conditions outside the scanned area. Calibration was more successful for sleeper displacement than for velocity and acceleration. These findings are not weaknesses to be hidden; they illustrate the role of open-loop uncertainty in real railway applications. A physics-assisted monitoring system must continuously update its boundary conditions and quantify the discrepancy between the model and the measured asset before its indicator can be used to trigger maintenance automatically.

The studies by Rahman et al. (2024), Ghiasi et al. (2025) and Milosevic et al. (2022) can thus be read as a connected sequence. DAS expands temporal and spatial coverage, drive-by monitoring uses operational vehicles to acquire repeated line-scale responses, domain adaptation supports knowledge transfer between lines, and asset-specific sensing supplies local diagnostic resolution. Together they define a multi-scale perception architecture. The unresolved issue is how to coordinate these levels so that a weak corridor-scale anomaly can initiate targeted inspection, obtain a mechanism-oriented diagnosis and produce an executable work order.
From Geometric Exceedance to Condition Interpretation and State Evolution

After perception, the next requirement is to transform measured abnormalities into infrastructure states. Conventional geometry inspection is highly effective for identifying where alignment, level, gauge or twist exceed specified limits. Nevertheless, the measured geometry is the combined consequence of the rail, fasteners, sleepers, ballast, subgrade, drainage, environmental exposure and maintenance history. Intelligent assessment must therefore progress from threshold exceedance to component inference, hidden-state diagnosis and evolution modelling.

Sresakoolchai and Kaewunruen (2022) demonstrated the first stage of this progression by combining track geometry measurements, component-defect records and track-profile data. Their case covered a 30-km section measured at one-foot intervals over four years from 2016 to 2019. Supervised models were used to identify rail, rail-joint, fastener and switch-and-crossing defects, while clustering and association-rule analysis were used to explore relationships among defect types and track characteristics. The best-performing deep neural network achieved approximately 94% accuracy. More important than the individual accuracy value is the change in the function of the data: geometry records collected for quality assessment were reused to infer component-level conditions that would otherwise require additional manual inspection.

This form of data reuse can increase the value of existing inspection systems without requiring immediate replacement of the sensing platform. However, it also shifts the bottleneck toward data governance. Component-defect labels must be spatially synchronized with geometry records, and differences in inspection timing can introduce false associations. Rare but safety-critical defects may be underrepresented, while high aggregate accuracy can conceal poor sensitivity for individual classes. The model output should therefore be interpreted as diagnostic evidence for targeted reinspection rather than as an autonomous maintenance command.

Wang, Liu and Euston (2023) extended geometry-based interpretation further by integrating track geometry defects with substructure and operational information on a passenger railroad in the United States. Their framework combined GPR-derived ballast-condition variables, rail-seat abrasion, traffic density, track class, curvature and maintenance-related information to estimate the risk of geometry-defect occurrence. This case changes the diagnostic question from "which component defect accompanies the measured geometry?" to "which underlying support and operating conditions make geometry defects more likely?" It therefore represents a transition from component classification to hidden-state and risk interpretation.
Figure The Framework for Estimation of Track Geometry Defect Risk(Wang, Liu and Euston, 2023)

The integration framework in Wang et al. is particularly relevant to the proposed first loop because it shows that data fusion is not merely the concatenation of sensor channels. Geometry, GPR, rail-seat abrasion, traffic and track-class data possess different spatial resolutions and reference systems. They must be segmented, registered and converted into consistent features before a data-driven risk model can be established. The case thus provides an engineering counterpart to the multi-source fusion concept discussed earlier in this paper.

The residual limitation is causal ambiguity. A geometry defect may result from ballast fouling, local stiffness variation, rail-seat abrasion, drainage failure or interacting causes. A predictive model can identify statistical risk without proving a unique deterioration mechanism. Consequently, its output should be used to guide additional inspection and maintenance prioritization. The precision intervention loop requires one further step: converting a high-risk section into a justified treatment type, such as tamping, ballast cleaning, drainage improvement, sleeper treatment or subgrade reinforcement.

Environmental cases broaden the concept of hidden state from structural condition to external forcing. Roghani (2021) investigated a frost-susceptible track section over the winter-spring periods of 2019 and 2020 using thermistors, total-station surveys and track geometry measurements. The observations linked freezing-degree days, frost penetration, track-surface deformation and changes in profile and alignment roughness. The study showed that freeze-thaw cycling can alter both the magnitude and spatial distribution of track deformation, particularly near geotechnically sensitive features such as culverts.
Figure Plots show track surface deformation measured by using total station(Roghani, 2021)

This field evidence has two implications for state-evolution modelling. First, deterioration cannot always be represented by a stationary curve derived only from historical geometry measurements. The evolution law changes when moisture, frost depth and temperature cycles change. Second, prediction confidence should vary with environmental conditions. During a period of rapid thaw or exceptional temperature fluctuation, a model trained on ordinary operating data should express greater uncertainty and trigger denser observation.

Kampczyk and Dybeł (2021) provide a related asset-scale example through their turnout-oriented digital-twin foundation. Their monitoring station integrated an external sensor into an S49 rail and recorded rail-head temperature together with ambient temperature, humidity and light. Although the implementation does not yet constitute a complete operational digital twin, it demonstrates that environmental boundary conditions must form part of the asset-state representation. A turnout twin based only on nominal geometry would omit variables capable of explaining thermal expansion, measurement variation and weather-dependent deterioration.

The above cases form a coherent assessment chain. Geometry data can first be used to infer component defects, then integrated with substructure and operational variables to estimate deterioration risk, and finally interpreted within changing environmental boundary conditions. This progression is central to the "state evolution" philosophy: the objective is not only to describe the current track geometry, but to determine which mechanism is active, how confidently it has been identified and how the condition may evolve under future traffic and environmental loading.
From Predictive Decision-Making to Physical Intervention and Feedback

The output of state assessment has operational value only when it changes maintenance action. This requires a transition from diagnosis to timing, treatment selection and resource allocation. It also requires post-intervention monitoring, because an intelligent O&M system must learn whether the selected treatment changed the subsequent deterioration trajectory.

Praticò and Fedele (2025) examined the economic logic of railway predictive maintenance by comparing renewal, reactive maintenance and proactive maintenance under different degradation curves and sensing-system cost scenarios. Their analysis emphasizes that a higher intervention frequency is not automatically preferable. The optimal strategy depends on the shape of the degradation curve, the condition level at intervention, the resulting recovery and the cost of sensing and maintenance. The study therefore supplies an important decision layer between condition prediction and physical execution.
