Within the first loop, the contribution of this analysis is to convert "earlier detection" into a constrained maintenance decision. Continuous sensing has a cost, false alarms create unnecessary intervention, and premature maintenance can consume resources without producing proportional performance gains. Conversely, delayed intervention can accelerate deterioration and increase renewal costs. Predictive maintenance should therefore optimize the expected long-term outcome rather than minimize a single condition indicator. In practical deployment, the economic model must be connected with line availability, maintenance-window constraints, safety risk and the measured effectiveness of alternative treatments.

Fischer (2022) provides field evidence for the intervention and feedback side of the architecture. The study examined geogrid reinforcement on a test section of Hungarian mainline No. 1 between Kelenföld and the Hegyeshalom state border. The site was established in 2010, and its geometry was monitored through rail-head levelling from 2010 to 2014 and recording-car measurements from 2010 to 2021. Different geogrid and control subsections enabled the long-term comparison of geometry deterioration under accumulated traffic and repeated maintenance.

This case is more than an example of a reinforcement material. In the dual-loop context, it illustrates how a physical intervention can be evaluated by its influence on the future state trajectory. The maintenance action is not treated as the end of the process. Instead, subsequent geometry measurements are used to compare deterioration phases, traffic accumulation and the performance of treated and untreated sections. This is the type of feedback required to update deterioration models and future treatment selection.

The field evidence also demonstrates why intervention assessment is difficult. Drainage condition, water pockets, precipitation, ballast screening, traffic accumulation and repeated tamping all influence the measured geometry. A simple before-and-after comparison may therefore attribute too much of the observed change to the intervention itself. A closed-loop system should maintain a structured record of treatment type, location, date, environmental condition, traffic exposure and post-maintenance response. Such records would allow the maintenance model to distinguish immediate geometry recovery from long-term deterioration reduction.

Praticò and Fedele (2025) and Fischer (2022) together connect the two sides of the second loop. The former asks when predictive maintenance is economically justified, whereas the latter shows how the long-term effect of a physical intervention can be measured. The remaining integration task is to connect predicted risk and cost-benefit analysis to a specific executable treatment and then return the measured outcome to the model. Without this feedback, predictive maintenance remains a planning concept rather than a learning closed loop.
Heavy-Haul Railway Lines—China's Dazhun Line

Among various types of railway lines, heavy-haul railways undertake the long-distance transportation of bulk energy and materials, and are characterized by typical operational features of heavy axle load, high-density traffic operation, and large transport volume. The wheel-rail forces borne by the line structure are far higher than those of ordinary passenger and freight railways, leading to faster structural deterioration rate, more rapid defect development, and significantly higher difficulty and pressure of O&M management and control than ordinary railway lines. The core contradictions between the construction period and the O&M period are more prominently manifested, making heavy-haul railways the core engineering scenario for verifying new concepts and technologies of railway O&M. This paper presents the engineering case of the Dazhun Heavy-Haul Railway. Aiming at the pain points of the traditional O&M mode under long-term high-intensity operation, this case constructs a dual closed-loop intelligent O&M system of "general survey - decision making - precision maintenance" centered on state evolution. It not only provides a complete engineering technical path to solve the core management and control problems in the O&M period of heavy-haul railways, but also offers a practical implementable paradigm and theoretical reference for the innovation of O&M modes in the global railway industry during the transition from the construction period to the O&M period.

The Dazhun Railway is a Class I single-track heavy-haul electrified railway, with a total length of 264 km for the main line and 24 stations along the entire line. The line traverses an area with extremely complex geological conditions, passing through unfavorable geological sections such as dense goaf areas of coal mines, soft soil strata, and saline soil strata. Meanwhile, the line is located in a region with harsh climatic conditions, where the maximum diurnal temperature difference can exceed 20℃, the annual average temperature difference reaches 34℃, the extreme annual temperature range is close to 70℃, the minimum temperature can drop to -30℃, and the maximum temperature can reach 40℃. The schematic diagram of its operation environment is shown in Figure 11. The Dazhun Railway has undergone multiple ten-thousand-ton capacity expansion and reconstruction projects as well as second-line construction, resulting in continuous improvement of its transport capacity. At present, its annual transport capacity has reached 230 million tons. The sustained hundred-million-ton level high-intensity operation has kept the track structure under the action of cyclic loading with heavy axle load for a long time, and the deterioration of service performance has become increasingly prominent. This has greatly aggravated a series of problems such as train operation instability, operation speed limitation, and elevated traffic safety risks. During long-term line O&M practices, it has been found that the track defects of the Dazhun Railway are complex and diverse, mainly concentrated in rail spalling, sleeper cracks, ballast whitening, and loosening and failure of components. Among them, rail damage is dominated by transverse fissures, bolt hole cracks, wear, spalling, and side wear, and more than 80% of rail damage is concentrated in small-radius curve sections with a radius ranging from 400 m to 1000 m, which is highly consistent with the line operation conditions and horizontal and vertical profile characteristics.
Figure . Operation Environment of the Dazhun Railway

The traditional O&M mode adopted by the line mainly relies on monthly inspection by track inspection vehicles, daily manual inspection via on-board monitoring devices, and manual static inspection during maintenance skylights for track state detection. This type of detection mode can only capture the static state of the line at a single time node, and cannot realize continuous tracking and dynamic monitoring of the track state deterioration process, let alone advance prediction of the deterioration trend of the line state. Emergency disposal and maintenance can only be carried out after the defects occur, or even develop to a level that affects traffic safety, which is highly prone to safety risks caused by delayed maintenance. Meanwhile, the time-based planned maintenance mode cannot formulate differentiated maintenance strategies according to the actual service state and deterioration rate of different sections of the line, and can only implement unified maintenance across the entire line in accordance with a fixed cycle. This easily leads to "over-maintenance" in sections with favorable state, which not only causes waste of O&M resources and pushes up the full-life cycle O&M cost of the line, but may also damage the original stable state of the track structure due to excessive maintenance. For key sections with fast deterioration rate and high risks, "under-maintenance" is prone to occur, which cannot timely curb the development of defects, eventually leading to the evolution of minor defects into major structural damage and further aggravating safety risks.

Aiming at the above core pain points, the Dazhun Railway has constructed a brand-new intelligent O&M system with the overall goal of solving the problems of line operation safety and intelligent O&M, and realizing condition-based maintenance centered on state evolution. The core concept of the new O&M system is to shift the focus of O&M work from "evaluating whether the current state meets the standards" to "predicting whether the future state will deteriorate", which directly responds to the core demand of preventing and controlling state deterioration during the O&M period. The system has established a dual closed-loop intelligent O&M mode of "general survey - decision making - precision maintenance". Through the integration of multi-dimensional sensing technology, big data analysis, artificial intelligence and digital twin technology, a complete closed loop of data acquisition, centralized management, intelligent analysis, decision application, and feedback optimization is formed.

As the data foundation of the system, the general survey link realizes comprehensive and continuous capture of the track structure state through vehicle-mounted Beidou vibration-noise integrated monitoring terminals, static track measuring instruments, and trackside distributed rail creep displacement observers. It forms a multi-source data acquisition matrix for track state covering dynamic and static, real-time and offline conditions, providing basic data support for subsequent analysis and decision-making.

To accurately grasp the evolution law of track state and fundamentally solve the core O&M contradiction of "fear of state deterioration", the Dazhun Railway has constructed a full-dimensional system of state assessment and intelligent decision-making models focusing on the evolution law of service performance and deterioration and damage mechanism of the track structure. It has realized the core leap from "current state evaluation" to "evolution trend prediction", which is also the core link of the entire intelligent O&M system.

The system first established a comprehensive characterization system for the service state of heavy-haul railway track structures, and deeply revealed the characterization methods, evolution laws and damage mechanisms of three typical defects, namely track geometric irregularity, rail corrugation and ballast fouling, under dynamic operation conditions. A research system of deterioration mechanism covering the full track structure including rails and ballast has been formed, laying a solid theoretical foundation for state evolution prediction. On this basis, the system constructed a comprehensive evaluation index system for track state covering multi-physical parameters based on vibration and noise signals, and put forward multi-dimensional evaluation criteria centered on "static state" and "dynamic driving performance" respectively. The dynamic indicators mainly characterize the dynamic response of the track structure under train load, including vehicle-mounted acceleration, frequency domain modal parameters and wheel load reduction rate, while the static indicators focus on basic state parameters such as track geometry and material properties. The combination of the two realizes quantitative hierarchical assessment of the track structure state under complex environments. Aiming at different types of defects and structural deterioration characteristics of heavy-haul railway tracks, the system has separately developed intelligent decision-making technologies for special precision maintenance operations, forming full-scene precision maintenance decision-making capabilities covering rail grinding, ballast tamping and cleaning, and precision adjustment of track alignment and position. In terms of rail grinding O&M, the system constructed an intelligent decision-making mechanism for rail grinding cycle based on the estimation results of the remaining service life of rails. The decision-making logic is established with the current state of the rail, life degradation trend and safety risk boundary as the main line, and acceptable risk thresholds are set in combination with multiple safety evaluation indicators such as wheel-rail impact acceleration and contact stress. Three types of decision suggestions, namely "Immediate Grinding", "Scheduled Grinding" and "No Grinding Required", are output (as shown in Figure 13). Meanwhile, the effect of different grinding strategies on rail life extension and risk suppression is quantified, realizing precise decision-making of grinding timing, grinding depth and grinding frequency, and solving the industry pain points of under-grinding and over-grinding under the traditional fixed-cycle grinding mode.

In terms of ballasted track bed O&M, the system established a multi-field coupled, multi-source heterogeneous ballast state sensing system. Through the fusion analysis of vehicle-mounted vibration and noise data, laser point cloud data of ballast section, high-definition image data and internal acceleration sensing data, comprehensive identification of ballast fouling, contamination and elasticity deterioration is realized. On this basis, a decision-making model for ballast tamping and cleaning operations was constructed based on deep reinforcement learning theory (as shown in Figure 14). Based on the predicted geometric recovery, the dynamic optimization of operation timing, operation intensity and resource allocation is realized by constructing a "state-action-reward" framework. Meanwhile, with the remaining service life of track units as the core indicator, a maintenance resource allocation strategy under different operation modes is formulated. The optimal operation sections and operation schemes are determined with the number and duration of maintenance skylights as constraints, realizing efficient and dynamic decision-making of tamping and cleaning cycles.

In terms of track alignment maintenance, the system proposed a multi-objective design method for track precision adjustment schemes applicable to different scenarios such as daily precision maintenance, periodic overhaul, and speed-up precision adjustment. A design framework for track geometry maintenance schemes was constructed based on physics-informed neural networks, combined with constraint models of multiple track geometric parameters including standard management specifications, irregularity amplitude, and remaining adjustable amount. Aiming at the different objectives of "precise control of over-limit irregularities with minimized human and material costs" for daily precision maintenance and "optimization of overall line smoothness with reasonable adjustment cost" for line overhaul, the optimal balance between the dual objectives of "minimum adjustment amount" and "optimal Track Quality Index (TQI)" is achieved, realizing automatic and intelligent generation of multi-objective precision maintenance schemes for track alignment and position.

To ensure the stable operation of the dual closed-loop system of "general survey - decision making - precision maintenance", the Dazhun Railway has simultaneously constructed a data middle platform and a digital twin system for intelligent O&M of heavy-haul railway tracks (as shown in Figure 15), providing full-process technical support for the O&M concept centered on state evolution. In terms of data middle platform construction, the system integrates data from newly developed equipment including Beidou vibration-noise integrated monitoring terminals, static geometry general survey measuring instruments, and rail creep observers, as well as data resources from existing systems including track inspection vehicles, flaw detection trolleys, and permanent way management systems, providing high-quality, full-cycle data assets for the analysis of track state evolution laws and the training of life prediction models. In terms of digital twin system construction, the system takes the Building Information Modeling (BIM) model of the track structure as the base, combines with Geographic Information System (GIS) geographic information, and constructs a digital mapping highly consistent with the physical track, realizing dynamic update and visual presentation of the track state. The system has also built a complete knowledge graph of track service state. Adopting a combination of top-down and bottom-up approaches, it first defines the schema layer to determine the core concepts and correlation relationships such as track structure, service state, defect type, and O&M events, and then fills the data layer in the form of "entity-relationship-attribute" triples, constructing a complete knowledge network of track service state and providing visual simulation and deduction capabilities for the prediction of track state evolution. Ultimately, the digital twin system presents the track state assessment results, deterioration trend prediction, and O&M decision-making schemes to O&M personnel in an intuitive form through a 3D visual interface, forming a new O&M mode for heavy-haul railways.

Centering on the core contradiction of the railway industry in the long-term O&M period, the Dazhun Railway case has realized the fundamental transformation of heavy-haul railway track O&M from post-event disposal to pre-event prediction, from extensive maintenance to precision maintenance, and from time-based maintenance to condition-based maintenance through the construction of the dual closed-loop system of "general survey - decision making - precision maintenance" with the O&M concept centered on state evolution. This case embodies a mature and implementable intelligent O&M technology system for heavy-haul railways, and provides a replicable and scalable engineering practice path for the historic transformation of the global railway industry from the large-scale construction period to the long-term large-scale O&M period.

Data Fusion and Imputation for Railway–Bridge Monitoring Systems

In integrated railway–bridge monitoring systems for high-speed railways, multi-source data—including track geometry inspection, train dynamic response, and bridge structural health monitoring—form a critical basis for infrastructure condition assessment and maintenance decision-making; however, due to sensor deployment limitations, communication interruptions, equipment failures, and maintenance activities, missing data are pervasive and significantly degrade data quality and reliability, thereby constraining downstream tasks such as condition prediction and damage identification. In practice, missing data generally exhibit two patterns: random missing (RM), characterized by sporadic and independent data loss caused by transient disturbances (e.g., signal interference or packet loss), and non-random missing (NM), involving continuous data gaps arising from sensor outages, power failures, or planned maintenance, often forming “blackout” periods. To address these challenges, a low-rank autoregressive tensor completion method is adopted to reconstruct incomplete multi-source monitoring data by representing correlated railway–bridge measurements as a third-order tensor and jointly modeling global spatial–temporal coherence and local temporal dynamics; specifically, the low-rank constraint captures intrinsic redundancy and cross-sensor correlations, while the autoregressive component enforces temporal consistency within individual sensor sequences, and the resulting optimization problem is efficiently solved via the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) under data fidelity constraints. The approach is evaluated using hourly multi-sensor data over a 59-day period, with missingness simulated under RM (20% and 40%) and NM scenarios involving full-day data gaps; results show that reconstruction errors increase with higher missing ratios, and that RM cases consistently achieve lower errors than NM cases due to the greater difficulty of recovering long contiguous gaps, although temporal regularization provides reasonable extrapolation capability. Overall, the method achieves reconstruction accuracies exceeding 90% at 20% missing rates and above 75% at 40%, demonstrates strong robustness in handling blackout-type missing data, and maintains high computational efficiency through GPU-based parallelization, confirming its effectiveness and scalability for large-scale spatiotemporal data imputation in railway–bridge monitoring applications.

Line-Bridge Dynamic Data Mileage Correction

In absolute static inspection, the measured vertical profile mainly reflects the discrepancy between the designed and actual bridge alignment, and as bridge deflection increases with span length, the relatively small amplitude of track vertical irregularities is easily masked by the bridge geometry. Moreover, environmental influences such as temperature variation and wind loads lead to significant differences between static and dynamic inspection waveforms. In contrast, gauge signals obtained from static and dynamic measurements exhibit higher consistency and stability; therefore, static gauge data are commonly adopted as the reference, with gauge selected as the correction channel. Using a macro-micro mileage correction model to calibrate dynamic inspection data, as shown in the figure. Macroscopic mileage alignment is typically performed using a sliding-window strategy, in which the Pearson correlation coefficient is employed as the similarity metric. The dynamic matching window is slid along the signal at the sampling interval, while the search is constrained by centering on the static window mileage and limiting the range to twice the window length to avoid long-distance mismatches and ensure data integrity. After macroscopic alignment, microscopic correction is introduced to further refine local correspondence. Rather than performing point-wise matching, which is highly sensitive to noise, the signal is segmented based on extremum points, and the data between adjacent local maxima and minima are defined as extremum segments that serve as basic matching units, effectively suppressing noise while preserving waveform characteristics. Because corresponding extremum segments in static and dynamic data often contain different numbers of sampling points, direct one-to-one matching is infeasible; therefore, each segment is abstracted into a high-dimensional feature vector to enable similarity comparison. For extremum point matching, a reference extremum point and its adjacent segments are selected from the static data, and candidate extremum points in the dynamic data are identified within a local neighborhood. The cosine similarity between the corresponding extremum segments is then calculated, and the dynamic extremum point yielding the maximum similarity is selected as the final match, thereby achieving refined local alignment between static and dynamic inspection data.

Multi-Source Data Fusion Analysis for Beams

To achieve high-precision diagnosis of the service condition of bridge-end expansion devices, prior exploratory analysis of high-dimensional and nonlinear monitoring data is indispensable, as the absence of an a priori understanding of intrinsic data structures and fault representation patterns undermines both the physical interpretability and data-driven validity of subsequent diagnostic models. Accordingly, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) clustering and Tucker tensor decomposition are adopted as essential prerequisite steps for damage identification. From an instantaneous-state perspective, t-SNE-based manifold learning demonstrates a distinguishable mapping between monitoring data and bridge-end structural irregularities, thereby providing data-level evidence for the feasibility of explicit state evaluation models. From a temporal-correlation perspective, Tucker tensor decomposition further reveals that critical faults such as jamming are not manifested as isolated anomalies in individual sensor readings, but rather as fundamental alterations in the correlation patterns among multi-source monitoring parameters. The monitoring state of a bridge-end rail expansion regulator at time t can be represented by a high-dimensional vector composed of multiple sensor measurements; however, excessive dimensionality leads to increased computational burden, overfitting risks, and limited visualization capability. Linear dimensionality reduction methods, such as principal component analysis (PCA), often fail to preserve nonlinear structures and show weak discriminative performance. In contrast, t-SNE effectively captures both linear and nonlinear relationships by converting pairwise distances into conditional probabilities and fitting low-dimensional distributions to high-dimensional data via gradient-based optimization, resulting in more clearly separated clusters that facilitate subsequent clustering-based interpretation. Validation using dynamic inspection data collected between August 2022 and December 2023 confirms that t-SNE-based clustering provides clear discrimination among irregularity characteristics, particularly for gauge-related features. Furthermore, a multi-source data fusion framework combining Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KAN) with attention mechanisms is introduced to analyze parameter mapping relationships and identify damage. KAN decomposes complex multivariate functions into interpretable univariate components, enabling explicit mathematical representation of the mapping between monitoring parameters and key performance indicators, while attention mechanisms enhance the modeling of global dependencies. By establishing normal-state mapping relationships between bridge-end monitoring parameters and expansion regulator displacement indicators, abnormal correlation patterns induced by jamming faults can be effectively identified, providing a robust basis for service-state assessment.

TQI Prediction for Kilometer-Scale Bridges

For kilometer-scale bridges, the long-term condition of the track structure directly impacts operational safety and ride comfort, with the Track Quality Index (TQI) serving as a key indicator of track geometry. Accurate prediction of TQI dynamics is essential for effective maintenance planning and prolonging structural service life. TQI data exhibit strong temporal dependencies, reflecting both gradual deterioration from cumulative operational effects—such as bridge creep and ballast degradation—and periodic influences from seasonal temperature variations, thermal expansion, and maintenance operations, resulting in nonlinear and non-stationary behavior. To address these complexities, a hybrid Prophet–Transformer (P-T) model is employed. The Prophet component decomposes each segment’s time series into trend, seasonal, and special-event components, automatically capturing long-term tendencies, monthly periodicity, and effects of maintenance or extreme events, while managing outliers flexibly. The Transformer then models residual errors from Prophet forecasts, using the residual deviation ratio as an additional feature to enhance the representation of nonlinear patterns and temporal dependencies, effectively creating a richer two-dimensional input space for learning complex relationships. Kilometer-scale bridges are divided into physically meaningful segments—including main span ends, midspan continuous beams, transition spans, and tower-constrained areas—to reflect spatial heterogeneity in TQI evolution. For each segment, monthly TQI data from 2021–2022 are used for training, and 2023 data are reserved for validation, ensuring independent segment-specific modeling. Rolling-window validation demonstrates that the P-T hybrid model achieves high predictive performance across all segments, with overall accuracy exceeding 95% and peak accuracies above 98% for most segments. Slightly lower accuracy near expansion joints and tower-constrained zones is attributed to higher local nonlinearity and structural complexity; nevertheless, performance remains robust. By integrating macro-scale trend extraction with fine-grained temporal feature learning, this approach provides a scalable, accurate framework for TQI prediction on kilometer-scale bridges, supporting precise segment-level maintenance and condition management decisions.

Example of General Survey- Track Irregularity Census Technology Based on On-Board Vibration and Noise Sensing

In the "dual closed-loop" logic for constructing a new intelligent railway operation and maintenance system, census serves as the foundation and prerequisite. Its core objective is to achieve rapid, efficient, low-cost, and full-coverage preliminary screening of the service status of tracks across massive railway lines, so as to address the pain point of "fragmented sensing" and provide a data basis for subsequent precise decision-making and maintenance. While traditional dynamic inspection vehicles feature high efficiency, they are limited in quantity and high in cost, making it impossible to realize high-frequency, all-weather universal inspection. Static inspection, on the other hand, suffers from low efficiency and can hardly meet the operation requirements of long mileage and high density. Therefore, the development of on-board intelligent sensing technology based on in-service trains, which converts a large number of operating trains into "mobile sensors", has become a key path to break through the bottlenecks of current railway operation and maintenance.

This section systematically reviews the core research achievements of track vertical irregularity census technology based on multi-source on-board vibration and noise data. This research systematically addresses the key scientific and technical challenges, including the nonlinear mapping between on-board vibration and noise data of in-service trains and track irregularity service status, insufficient model generalization performance under small-scale labeled data, and poor engineering adaptability of detection results. A full-chain technical system covering data acquisition, intelligent inversion to decision support is constructed, which provides systematic theoretical support and an engineerable technical path for the implementation of the census link in the intelligent operation and maintenance system.
From Dedicated Inspection to Universal Sensing: A Fundamental Shift in Census Detection Philosophy

One of the core theoretical contributions of this research is the explicit proposal of a new census concept: "rapid identification of the service status of track irregularity using multi-source in-carriage vibration and noise data generated during the operation of in-service trains". The advantages of this concept are reflected in two aspects. The first is the fundamental transformation of the inspection subject, that is, the inspection task is shifted from expensive dedicated track inspection vehicles to a large number of high-speed electric multiple units (EMUs) and metro trains shuttling on the rail network daily. This makes high-frequency, low-cost full-coverage inspection possible, and promotes the leap from "regular physical examination" to "real-time health monitoring". The second is the innovation of sensing means: instead of relying on traditional dedicated precision sensors such as lasers, cameras or inertial navigation, low-cost and easy-to-install intelligent sensors installed in the carriage of in-service trains (such as the intelligent ride-along monitor independently developed by the research team) are used to collect "accompanying" data including car-body vibration acceleration and in-carriage noise. Although these data are not as direct as precision measurement data, they contain rich information on track status, and feature extremely low acquisition cost and easy large-scale deployment.
Deep Integration of Physics and Data: Resolving the Contradiction Between "Quality and Quantity" of Census Data

There is a complex nonlinear mapping relationship between the on-board vibration and noise data collected based on in-service trains and the track irregularity excitation. Meanwhile, in railway engineering scenarios, the high acquisition cost, small sample size and limited working condition coverage of labeled measured data are the core scientific problems restricting the accuracy and generalization performance of on-board inspection models. The research ingeniously constructs a "physics-data fusion" method combining physical models and data models, which effectively solves the contradiction between "quality and quantity" of data and provides core algorithm support for high-precision census.

Establishing a high-fidelity physical model to generate sufficient training data is the primary step to address the shortage of measured data. To compensate for the limitations of measured data and explore the inherent physical relationship between excitation and response, the team first established a vehicle-track coupled vibration and noise simulation model. The model can simulate the vehicle vibration and noise response under arbitrary track irregularity conditions, and generate massive, diverse and labeled simulation data as the "knowledge source" for model training. Among them, the vehicle-track rigid-flexible coupled dynamic model not only considers the multi-rigid-body vehicle model and flexible track (Timoshenko beam), but also introduces the flexible wheelset model. The finite element model (FEM) of the wheelset is simplified through Guyan reduction theory, as shown in Table 11. On the premise of ensuring the calculation accuracy, the accurate simulation of medium and high frequency wheel-rail vibration is realized. In addition, based on the three-dimensional spatial wave equation and implicit transient analysis method, the research established an acoustic model of wheelset vibration and noise, which can solve the transient response of the sound field under the action of wheelset vibration (Figure 20). This provides a physical basis for the subsequent identification of short-wave track irregularities (such as rail corrugation) using in-carriage noise data. Through the above physical models, the researchers can simulate simulation data sets under various working conditions including track irregularities with different wavelengths and amplitudes, providing abundant samples for the training of subsequent data models.

Developing an intelligent inversion model to achieve accurate mapping from response to excitation is the key to converting massive simulation data into practical technology. Targeted deep learning models are developed for different application scenarios. For the identification of medium and long wave (2-120m) track vertical irregularity in high-speed railways, the research proposes an Extended Auto-Encoder (EAE) neural network model as shown in Figure 21. The model has an ingenious structure: it compresses track irregularity information using an auto-encoder, then establishes the mapping between car-body acceleration and the compressed low-dimensional features through an estimator network, and finally decodes and reconstructs the irregularity waveform. This design effectively reduces the difficulty of direct end-to-end learning, and improves the robustness and generalization performance of the model. In the verification of measured data under different working conditions such as bridge, tunnel and subgrade sections, the EAE model performs significantly better than the traditional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). As shown in Table 12, under the training of measured data, the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of the EAE model is 23% lower than that of the CNN model on average; after the introduction of physics-data fusion, its MAPE is as low as 1%~2%, demonstrating excellent waveform identification accuracy.

From Point Estimation to Interval Estimation: Improving the Reliability and Decision-Making Value of Census Results

Most traditional track irregularity inversion models output results in the form of point estimation, which cannot quantify the uncertainty of model prediction and can hardly meet the risk control requirements of railway operation and maintenance decision-making. The research introduces Bayesian Deep Learning (BDL) into track irregularity identification, and approximates variational inference through the Monte Carlo Dropout method, successfully realizing interval estimation of track irregularity. This innovation enables the output of the model to be no longer a single waveform, but an estimation range including confidence intervals, providing richer information for decision makers. When the estimation interval is narrow and covers the real value, it indicates that the model's evaluation result for this section is relatively certain; when the estimation interval is wide, it means that the model has great uncertainty, and recheck combined with more information (such as precision measurement) is required. More importantly, interval estimation makes operation and maintenance decision-making more conservative and reliable.

In bridge sections, the EAE model after physics-data fusion achieves a Coverage Width Error (CWE) of 0.91 for interval estimation, which is much higher than 0.81 of the CNN model. This means that the EAE model can not only accurately estimate the irregularity waveform, but also give a high-confidence prediction interval, effectively avoiding the risk of missed detection caused by underestimated point estimation results.

Research Background and Research Purpose

With the gradual transformation of the railway industry from the large-scale construction stage to the long-term safe operation and maintenance stage, the rail, as the core bearing component of railway transportation, its operation state detection and maintenance quality are directly related to the safety, stability and efficiency of railway transportation. Therefore, the demand for intelligent, efficient and precise rail inspection and maintenance in the industry has become increasingly prominent. Traditional manual inspection methods are affected by various factors such as the operator's skill level, sense of responsibility, fatigue and on-site environment (such as bad weather and complex terrain), which not only result in low inspection efficiency and high labor costs, but also make it difficult to effectively integrate and conduct linkage analysis of multi-source detection data, leading to problems such as missed inspection and false inspection. Single-function inspection equipment, on the other hand, has limitations such as limited detection dimensions, poor data compatibility and inability to achieve full-process detection coverage. Neither of them can meet the actual needs of full-process intelligent operation and maintenance including rail defect localization, detection, measurement and evaluation, nor can they support the development trend of intelligent transformation of railway operation and maintenance. In response to the above industry pain points and research gaps, research teams in the field of rail intelligent operation and maintenance have focused on relevant technological breakthroughs, and combined with the core needs of the "Dual Closed-Loop" intelligent operation and maintenance system proposed in this paper, developed a multi-sensor integrated track self-inspection robot, which is used as the core implementation carrier of the "Dual Closed-Loop" intelligent operation and maintenance system to mainly solve the key technical problems of synchronous acquisition and high-precision integration of multi-source data in rail inspection. The core function of the robot is to realize high-precision, comprehensive and synchronous collection of rail status data, providing reliable and comprehensive data support for the full-process operation and maintenance decision-making of the "Dual Closed-Loop" system, and helping railway operation and maintenance transform from "passive emergency repair" to "proactive prediction and precise operation and maintenance", which is also the core original intention of the robot's research and development. At the same time, the research and development and application of this case can directly support the core viewpoint of "intelligent equipment empowering the upgrading of railway operation and maintenance" proposed in this paper, providing solid empirical support for the research conclusions of the paper.
Overall Design of the Robot

To adapt to the needs of rail intelligent inspection and effectively support the landing application of the "Dual Closed-Loop" intelligent operation and maintenance system proposed in this paper, the overall design of the robot adopts the design concept of modularization, lightweight and high adaptability, with the core research and development goal clearly defined as "providing stable and accurate multi-source data support for the 'Dual Closed-Loop' system". Based on this goal, the robot is integrally designed into two core parts: a mobile carrier platform and a multi-source data acquisition system. This modular design scheme is determined after multiple rounds of scheme demonstration and optimization, which not only facilitates the disassembly, transportation and on-site deployment of the equipment, reduces the operation difficulty of maintenance personnel, but also can flexibly adjust the sensor configuration according to the actual needs of on-site inspection and the data acquisition requirements of the "Dual Closed-Loop" system, improving the versatility and scalability of the equipment, and solving the problem that traditional inspection equipment has fixed functions and is difficult to adapt to different operation and maintenance scenarios. Among them, the core of the mobile carrier platform design is to ensure the stable operation of the robot in complex track environments and provide reliable mobile support for data acquisition. For this reason, a lightweight symmetrical hollow frame structure is adopted, which not only balances structural stability and portability, but also effectively reduces the impact of the robot's own weight on the track. To adapt to the operation needs of tracks of different types, the platform is equipped with high-strength load-bearing wheels and adaptively adjustable limit mechanisms. By optimizing the telescopic logic of the limit mechanisms, they can flexibly expand and contract according to changes in rail gauge, ensuring that the robot can run stably on tracks of different types and working conditions, avoiding operation deviations caused by differences in track specifications, and ensuring the stability of data acquisition. The driving system selects high-performance hub motors, and realizes stable and constant speed driving of the robot by optimizing the motor control algorithm, which can not only meet the needs of efficient inspection and shorten the inspection cycle, but also facilitate maintenance personnel to follow up operations on site and handle equipment abnormalities in a timely manner, providing convenient support for the on-site operation and maintenance link of the "Dual Closed-Loop" system. This series of designs are targeted research and development carried out in combination with the actual rail inspection scenarios and the needs of the "Dual Closed-Loop" system, directly serving the intelligent operation and maintenance concept proposed in the paper.

Design and Development of Multi-Source Data Acquisition System

The multi-source data acquisition system is the core functional module of the robot, and its performance directly determines the accuracy and comprehensiveness of data acquisition, thus affecting the scientificity of the decision-making of the "Dual Closed-Loop" intelligent operation and maintenance system. For this reason, the core of the system's research and development is positioned as "multi-sensor collaboration, high-precision acquisition, and real-time processing and fusion" to meet the full-dimensional needs of the "Dual Closed-Loop" system for rail status data. The system selects a high-performance embedded computing unit as the core control unit, which is determined to have strong parallel computing capabilities and real-time data processing capabilities after multiple rounds of test and selection, and can realize synchronous reception, real-time processing and fusion analysis of multi-sensor data, solving the problems of low processing efficiency and large data delay of traditional data acquisition systems. To realize full-dimensional acquisition of rail status data, the system integrates various high-precision sensors, including laser radar, line laser profile scanner, combined navigation system, industrial camera and inline odometer. The selection of each sensor is strictly tested and demonstrated to ensure its stable performance and complementary functions, which can cover all key dimensions of rail status detection: laser radar is used to quickly obtain 3D spatial information of the rail surrounding environment, providing data support for the environmental perception link of the "Dual Closed-Loop" system; line laser profile scanner is used to accurately capture the rail cross-sectional profile and wear details, providing core data for rail defect detection and status evaluation; combined navigation system is used to real-time obtain the precise position information of the robot, providing reliable support for defect localization, ensuring that the "Dual Closed-Loop" system can accurately locate the defect position and carry out subsequent operation and maintenance work; industrial camera is used to collect rail surface images to assist in identifying subtle defects on the rail surface; inline odometer is used to assist in positioning, improving the position accuracy of the robot. Through optimizing the installation layout of sensors and data transmission protocols, the collaborative work of various sensors is realized, fully ensuring the accuracy and comprehensiveness of data acquisition, and providing core data support for the full-process application of the "Dual Closed-Loop" intelligent operation and maintenance system. The design and development achievements directly support the research viewpoint of "multi-source data fusion empowering intelligent operation and maintenance" in this paper.

Multi-Sensor Integration Framework and Experimental Verification

The synchronization and consistency of multi-source data are the key to ensuring the accuracy of data fusion, and also the premise for the "Dual Closed-Loop" intelligent operation and maintenance system to achieve accurate decision-making. Aiming at the key technical problems such as time asynchrony and spatial misalignment in the process of multi-sensor data fusion, relevant research and development work has focused on technological breakthroughs, and built a multi-sensor integration framework based on the ROS system, which effectively solves the above technical bottlenecks and lays a solid foundation for data fusion analysis. This technological innovation further supports the technical research content of this paper. In terms of time synchronization, a professional synchronization mechanism is adopted to add unified timestamps to various sensor data. At the same time, to solve the problem of timestamp misalignment caused by differences in sampling frequencies of different sensors, an interpolation algorithm is designed and adopted to accurately correct the timestamps, realizing precise time synchronization of multi-source data, ensuring that data collected by different sensors can correspond to the same inspection moment, and improving the accuracy of data fusion. In terms of spatial calibration, a large number of calibration experiments are carried out to complete the internal parameter calibration of each sensor and the external parameter calibration between sensors. By optimizing the calibration method, the calibration accuracy is improved, making it much lower than the industry standard, fully meeting the requirements of data fusion accuracy, and ensuring that data collected by different types of sensors such as laser radar, camera and inertial navigation can be accurately aligned in the same spatial coordinate system, providing reliable guarantee for subsequent data fusion analysis. To verify the feasibility and practicality of the robot and provide empirical support for the research conclusions of this paper, a series of systematic experimental verifications are carried out. The experimental scenarios cover different types of test tracks and actual operating lines, including various rail gauges, different operating conditions and complex environmental scenarios, comprehensively simulating the actual situation of on-site rail inspection. During the experiment, the data acquisition stability, battery life, environmental adaptability and data support capability of the robot are focused on testing. The experimental results show that the robot can stably collect various types of rail status data, its battery life can meet the continuity requirements of on-site rail inspection, it has strong environmental adaptability, and can run stably in complex track environments.
Application Value of the Robot and Its Support for the Paper

More importantly, the multi-source data collected by the robot can effectively support the full-process application of the "Dual Closed-Loop" intelligent operation and maintenance system, which is not only the core goal of the robot's research and development, but also the key to its support for the content of this paper. Specifically, the high-precision point cloud data and image data collected by the robot can provide reliable support for the semantic map construction and combined positioning links of the "Dual Closed-Loop" system, realizing high-precision positioning and ensuring that the system can accurately grasp the spatial position information of the rail. The rail cross-sectional profile data and surface image data collected can support the system to carry out rail wear state recognition and robust defect detection, timely find various potential defects of the rail, and provide core data for the detection and early warning link of the "Dual Closed-Loop" system. The defect characteristic data collected can provide accurate support for risk assessment based on vehicle-track coupling dynamics, helping the system to accurately predict the risk of rail defects and provide a scientific basis for operation and maintenance decision-making. In addition, verified by experimental comparison, compared with traditional inspection methods and single-function inspection equipment, the robot has significant advantages in inspection efficiency, detection accuracy, data comprehensiveness and other aspects, which can effectively improve the efficiency and accuracy of rail inspection and maintenance, and further confirm the feasibility and superiority of the "Dual Closed-Loop" intelligent operation and maintenance system proposed in this paper. In summary, the multi-sensor integrated track self-inspection robot has effectively solved the key problems of synchronous acquisition and high-precision integration of multi-source data in rail inspection through targeted design, research and development and experimental verification. Its modular design and stable performance can adapt to complex track environments, and can provide comprehensive and high-precision data support for the "Dual Closed-Loop" intelligent operation and maintenance system. At the same time, the research and development and application of this case provide solid empirical support for the research viewpoint of rail intelligent operation and maintenance in this paper, confirm the application value of intelligent equipment in the field of rail operation and maintenance, and promote the development of intelligent transformation of railway operation and maintenance, which is also the core significance of the development of work related to this case.

In conclusion, this paper provides a comprehensive synthesis of the evolving paradigms governing the intelligent operation and maintenance of large-scale railway infrastructures. As global rail networks transition from a phase of intensive construction to one of long-term sustainable asset management, the inherent limitations of traditional maintenance models have become increasingly apparent. These constraints include spatial-temporal blind spots in macroscopic monitoring, the superficial nature of existing sensing technologies, and the inherent lag of reactive decision making, all of which necessitate a fundamental shift toward more proactive AI driven strategies to ensure the safety and reliability of complex railway systems.

To address these critical bottlenecks, this study has proposed a pioneering top-level architecture rooted in the "State Evolution" philosophy. This framework is characterized by two synergetic and continuous cycles that bridge the gap between abstract data and physical maintenance. The first cycle, an AI-driven full-process intelligent O&M closed loop, integrates wideband geometric perception with multi-source feature fusion to achieve a holistic characterization of infrastructure health. Complementing this, the second cycle serves as a precision intervention loop, utilizing AI agents and autonomous robotic systems to translate diagnostic insights into targeted, high-precision physical interventions, thereby optimizing resource allocation and extending system longevity.

Specifically, the implementation of track-coupled dynamics monitoring on the Dazhun Heavy-Haul Railway and the development of multi-sensor integrated inspection robots demonstrate a successful paradigm shift from "evaluating current states" to "predicting future deterioration." These case studies that the proposed framework not only enhances the accuracy of fault detection but also provides a robust, scalable roadmap for integrating advanced artificial intelligence into the demanding and unstructured environments of heavy-haul and high-speed rail operations.

Looking ahead, the evolution of intelligent railway O&M will be driven by the deep convergence of several frontier technologies. The integration of domain-specific multimodal large models will be essential for enhancing the interpretive power and robustness of the intelligent O&M closed loop, while the advancement of embodied intelligence will further refine the execution capabilities of the precision intervention loop. Furthermore, the development of high-fidelity digital twins will enable real-time simulation of complex degradation processes, allowing for the optimization of predictive maintenance schedules before physical failures occur. Collectively, the theoretical framework and practical pathways outlined in this paper establish a strategic foundation for the next generation of resilient, autonomous, and sustainable railway infrastructure management systems.
